entries.text: microsoft onenote screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft onenote screen reader manual notes, notebooks, pages, and organization independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft screen reader support for onenote purpose: this manual teaches current microsoft onenote from the beginning to a person using a screen reader. it explains what to press, where focus should move, what should be announced, and how to recover when the result is different. reference version: the main procedures are written for the current onenote desktop app included with microsoft 365 on windows. separate sections cover onenote for the web, macos/voiceover, mobile, and braille. important version note: the former onenote for windows 10 app reached end of support in october 2025. this guide therefore focuses on the current desktop onenote app rather than the retired windows 10 app. how to use this manual learn onenote's structure first: notebook, section, page, page title, and content block. use ctrl+g to move to the notebook picker, ctrl+shift+g to move to sections, and ctrl+alt+g to move to pages. press ctrl+t to create a section and ctrl+n to create a page in the current section. press tab from a page title to move into the page content area. onenote pages can contain several independent note containers; screen readers may announce them as content blocks. use ctrl+e to search all notebooks and ctrl+f to search the current page. use ctrl+1 through ctrl+9 for common note tags; ctrl+0 removes note tags from selected notes. use f9 to synchronize all shared notebooks and shift+f9 to synchronize the current shared notebook. save is normally automatic because onenote synchronizes notebook changes. before sharing, verify which notebook you are sharing and whether it contains private sections/pages. table of contents part 1 - what onenote is part 2 - open onenote and learn the structure part 3 - switch notebooks part 4 - create and navigate sections part 5 - create and navigate pages part 6 - page titles and content blocks part 7 - type, edit, and format notes part 8 - lists and outlines part 9 - note tags part 10 - tables part 11 - links, files, pictures, and alt text part 12 - search onenote part 13 - audio notes part 14 - move, copy, rename, and delete pages/sections part 15 - section groups part 16 - sharing and collaboration part 17 - sync and offline behavior part 18 - accessibility checker and accessible notebook design part 19 - narrator with onenote part 20 - nvda with onenote part 21 - jaws with onenote part 22 - voiceover and onenote for mac part 23 - onenote for the web part 24 - braille displays part 25 - iphone/ipad and android part 26 - security and privacy part 27 - troubleshooting part 28 - independent practice course part 29 - quick reference commands part 30 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what onenote is onenote is a digital notebook application. information is organized in a hierarchy rather than as separate files for every note. notebook: the top-level collection of notes. section: a major category within a notebook. section group: an optional folder-like grouping of sections. page: one note page inside a section. subpage: a page visually/structurally nested beneath another page. page title: the page's name and a key navigation cue. content block: a note container on the page. one page can contain several. tag: a marker such as to do, important, question, or contact. shared notebook: a notebook stored where other authorized people can collaborate. part 2 - open onenote and learn the structure 2.1 open onenote what you will learn: start onenote without using a mouse. before you begin: onenote must be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type onenote. press enter on microsoft onenote. wait for the app to open. press ctrl+g. listen for the current notebook. press ctrl+shift+g. listen for the current section. press ctrl+alt+g. listen for the current page. what should happen: you can identify the notebook, section, and page layers. if that does not happen: if one shortcut does not move focus, press escape to close menus/dialogs and try again. practice: open onenote and identify notebook, section, and page. focus map: notebook, section, page, page title, and page content are separate focus locations. when a command behaves unexpectedly, identify which layer currently has focus. part 3 - switch notebooks 3.1 switch to another open notebook what you will learn: move between notebooks without hunting through the interface. before you begin: have more than one notebook open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g. use up/down arrow through the notebook list. listen to each notebook name. press spacebar on the notebook you want. wait for its last visited page to open. press ctrl+shift+g to verify its sections. what should happen: the selected notebook becomes active. if that does not happen: if only one notebook is listed, another notebook has not been opened/synced into this onenote profile. practice: switch between two notebooks and return. part 4 - create and navigate sections 4.1 create a section what you will learn: add a major category to the current notebook. before you begin: open the notebook where the section belongs. exactly how to do it press ctrl+t. listen for the new section name text box. type a descriptive section name. press enter. what should happen: a new section is created and named. if that does not happen: if a new page appears unexpectedly, confirm you pressed ctrl+t rather than ctrl+n. practice: create a section named practice. 4.2 navigate sections what you will learn: move directly through section tabs. before you begin: the notebook has multiple sections. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+g. use up/down arrow through sections as announced in your current layout. stop on the desired section. press spacebar or enter if necessary to activate it. press ctrl+alt+g to move to that section's pages. what should happen: the selected section becomes active and its pages are available. if that does not happen: if arrows move within page text, ctrl+shift+g did not move focus to sections. practice: move through every section once. part 5 - create and navigate pages 5.1 create a page what you will learn: add a new note page to the current section. before you begin: select the correct section first. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n. listen for a new untitled page and page-title field. type a descriptive page title. press enter. begin typing page content. what should happen: a new page is created at the end of the current section. if that does not happen: if a new application window opens, verify the onenote window had focus. practice: create pages named meeting notes and ideas. 5.2 navigate pages what you will learn: move among pages without searching. before you begin: the section has several pages. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+g. use up/down arrow through page titles. press spacebar or enter on the desired page. listen for the page title. press tab once to move into the content area. what should happen: the desired page opens and you can reach its notes. if that does not happen: if ctrl+alt+g does not move to pages, close any dialog and try again. practice: move among five pages and return to the first. part 6 - page titles and content blocks 6.1 jump to the page title what you will learn: rename or review the page's title. before you begin: a page is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+t. listen for the page title. edit the title if needed. press enter. press tab to move into the page content. what should happen: focus moves to the page title and then back to content. if that does not happen: if ctrl+shift+t affects selected text instead, make sure onenote—not a browser—is active. practice: rename a practice page and rename it back. 6.2 move between content blocks what you will learn: understand onenote's free-form note containers. before you begin: a page contains more than one note container. exactly how to do it press ctrl+a three times to select all content blocks on the page. press tab to move among the selected content blocks. press shift+tab to move backward. press escape to cancel the block selection when finished. what should happen: focus cycles among note containers rather than only within one line of text. if that does not happen: if ctrl+a selects only text, press it additional times as documented until page content blocks are selected. practice: create two separate note containers and move between them. beginner recommendation: for predictable screen-reader reading order, keep most notes in one main vertical content block unless separate containers are truly useful. part 7 - type, edit, and format notes task command bold ctrl+b italic ctrl+i underline ctrl+u undo / redo ctrl+z / ctrl+y copy / cut / paste ctrl+c / ctrl+x / ctrl+v select all / expand selection ctrl+a, press again as needed left align ctrl+l right align ctrl+r 7.1 edit a note what you will learn: correct existing text precisely. before you begin: place the caret in page text. exactly how to do it use ctrl+left/right arrow to move by word. use left/right arrow to move by character. use backspace or delete to remove incorrect text. type the correction. press ctrl+z if the change occurs in the wrong location. what should happen: only the intended text changes. if that does not happen: if arrow keys move between onenote interface elements, return to the page content area with tab/f6 as appropriate. practice: create and correct three errors. 7.2 apply formatting what you will learn: format selected text without retyping it. before you begin: select a practice phrase. exactly how to do it press ctrl+b. move the caret into the formatted text. use your screen reader's formatting-information command if available. press ctrl+b again to remove bold when desired. what should happen: the selected text toggles bold formatting. if that does not happen: if newly typed text stays bold unintentionally, press ctrl+b once more to turn bold off. practice: bold, italicize, and underline separate phrases. part 8 - lists and outlines task command bulleted list ctrl+period numbered list ctrl+forward slash or ctrl+shift+o increase indent/outline level tab decrease indent/outline level shift+tab move paragraph up/down alt+shift+up / alt+shift+down increase/decrease paragraph indent alt+shift+right / alt+shift+left 8.1 create a bulleted list what you will learn: create a structured list of related notes. before you begin: place the caret on a blank line. exactly how to do it press ctrl+period. type the first item. press enter. type the second item. press enter. type the third item. press enter twice or toggle the list command off to leave the list. what should happen: onenote creates a bulleted list. if that does not happen: if a period is typed instead of creating a list, confirm ctrl is held with the period key. practice: create a three-item list. 8.2 create an outline what you will learn: build hierarchical notes. before you begin: start a bulleted or plain-text outline. exactly how to do it type a top-level item and press enter. press tab to indent one level. type a subordinate item. press enter. press shift+tab to return one level. use alt+shift+up/down to reorder selected paragraphs. what should happen: the note structure gains levels that can be collapsed/expanded in supported contexts. if that does not happen: if tab inserts a tab character, place the caret at the beginning of the paragraph/list item. practice: create a two-level outline. part 9 - note tags task command to do ctrl+1 important ctrl+2 question ctrl+3 remember for later ctrl+4 definition ctrl+5 highlight ctrl+6 contact ctrl+7 address ctrl+8 phone number ctrl+9 remove selected note tags ctrl+0 9.1 apply a to do tag what you will learn: turn a line into a trackable task marker. before you begin: place the caret in a note line. exactly how to do it press ctrl+1. listen for the tag/checkbox announcement if your screen reader reports it. press ctrl+1 again when you want to mark/select/clear the to do state according to the current note context. use ctrl+0 when you need to remove tags from selected notes. what should happen: the note is tagged as a to do item. if that does not happen: if the shortcut produces a literal number, the page content may not have focus. practice: tag three action items. part 10 - tables 10.1 create a quick table what you will learn: turn typed text into a table with tab. before you begin: place the caret on a blank line. exactly how to do it type the first cell text. press tab. type the next cell. press tab. continue entering cells. when the caret is in the last table cell, press tab to create another cell/row. use ctrl+enter inside a table cell when you intentionally want to insert a row below. what should happen: onenote creates and extends a table. if that does not happen: if tab simply indents text, the initial context may not be creating a table; use insert > table instead. practice: create a 3-column table with two data rows. accessibility: keep onenote tables simple. avoid using a complex table when headings or lists would communicate the information more clearly. part 11 - links, files, pictures, and alt text 11.1 insert a hyperlink what you will learn: create useful linked text. before you begin: select meaningful text. exactly how to do it press ctrl+k. enter or paste the destination address. press enter. read the linked phrase and confirm it describes the destination. what should happen: the selected text becomes a hyperlink. if that does not happen: if the visible text is only a long raw url, replace it with descriptive text when the url itself is not needed. practice: create one descriptive link. 11.2 add alt text to a picture what you will learn: describe a meaningful image. before you begin: insert or select a picture. exactly how to do it open the picture's context menu with shift+f10. find the alt text or accessibility-related command available in your version. enter a concise description of the image's purpose/content. close the pane/dialog. what should happen: the image has alternative text for screen-reader users. if that does not happen: if alt text is not available in the context menu, use the ribbon or accessibility checker to reach the control. practice: add alt text to a practice image. embedded files: microsoft accessibility guidance recommends alternative text for important visuals and embedded files, along with meaningful link text and descriptive section/page names. part 12 - search onenote task command search all notebooks ctrl+e search current page ctrl+f 12.1 search all notebooks what you will learn: find a note even when you do not remember where it is stored. before you begin: know one distinctive word or phrase. exactly how to do it press ctrl+e. type the search term. use arrow keys through results. listen for notebook/section/page context when announced. press enter on the desired result. what should happen: onenote opens the matching page/result. if that does not happen: if results are too broad, type a more distinctive phrase or narrow the search scope from the search controls. practice: search for one word across several notebooks. 12.2 search the current page what you will learn: locate one phrase on a long page. before you begin: open a page with several paragraphs. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. type the phrase. move through matches. press escape when finished. what should happen: onenote highlights/navigates matching text on the current page. if that does not happen: if the search finds results elsewhere, verify you used ctrl+f rather than ctrl+e. practice: find three terms on one page. part 13 - audio notes task command start a new audio recording ctrl+alt+a play selected audio ctrl+alt+p stop audio playback ctrl+alt+s back 10 seconds ctrl+alt+y forward 10 seconds ctrl+alt+u 13.1 record an audio note what you will learn: capture audio associated with a page. before you begin: use a non-confidential practice notebook and confirm microphone permission. exactly how to do it place the caret where the recording should be associated. press ctrl+alt+a. speak a short practice sentence. use the recording controls to stop recording. select the audio item. press ctrl+alt+p to play it. press ctrl+alt+s to stop playback. what should happen: an audio recording is attached to the page and can be played. if that does not happen: if recording does not start, check microphone permissions and whether another application is using the microphone. practice: record and play a short harmless note. privacy: audio recording can capture people who did not expect to be recorded. follow consent, workplace, school, and local legal requirements. part 14 - move, copy, rename, and delete pages/sections 14.1 move a page up or down what you will learn: reorder pages in the current section. before you begin: focus the page list. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+g. use up/down arrow to select the page. press shift+alt+up or shift+alt+down. listen for the page's new position. what should happen: the page moves within the section. if that does not happen: if the text paragraph moves instead, focus is still in page content rather than the page list. practice: move a practice page and move it back. 14.2 delete a page what you will learn: remove a page deliberately. before you begin: focus the page in the page list. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+g. select the disposable page. press shift+f10. move to delete page. activate it. confirm if prompted. what should happen: the page is removed. if that does not happen: always read the page title before deleting. shared notebooks may affect other collaborators. practice: create and delete a disposable page. 14.3 move a section what you will learn: reorder sections within a notebook. before you begin: focus the sections pane. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+g. select the section. press shift+alt+up or shift+alt+down. listen for the new order. what should happen: the section changes position. if that does not happen: if the command changes a paragraph, return to the sections pane. practice: move the practice section and restore its position. part 15 - section groups 15.1 create a section group what you will learn: group related sections in a large notebook. before you begin: open a notebook with several sections. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+g. press shift+f10. move to new section group. press spacebar or enter. type a descriptive group name. press enter. what should happen: a new section group is created. if that does not happen: if the context menu opens for a page, press ctrl+shift+g before retrying. practice: create a section group named archive practice. 15.2 move a section into a section group what you will learn: organize existing sections. before you begin: focus the section. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+g. select the section. press shift+f10. choose move or copy. find the destination section group. select it and complete the move action. what should happen: the section moves into the section group. if that does not happen: if you need the section in both places, use copy rather than move when the dialog offers it. practice: move a practice section and return it. part 16 - sharing and collaboration 16.1 share a notebook what you will learn: give another person access to a notebook rather than a single isolated page. before you begin: use a notebook appropriate for sharing. exactly how to do it open the share command from the ribbon/file area. enter the recipient's email address. review the permission level offered by your microsoft 365/onedrive/sharepoint environment. read the notebook name again. add a message if needed. activate send/share. what should happen: the recipient receives access according to the selected permission. if that does not happen: onenote sharing is generally notebook-based. do not share a notebook that contains private sections just because one page is safe. practice: inspect sharing controls on a practice notebook without sending. collaboration: shared notebooks can synchronize other people's edits. use descriptive page/section names so collaborators can navigate changes efficiently. part 17 - sync and offline behavior task command synchronize all shared notebooks f9 synchronize current shared notebook shift+f9 17.1 force a sync what you will learn: check whether recent changes synchronize. before you begin: use a notebook stored in onedrive or sharepoint. exactly how to do it press shift+f9 to sync the current shared notebook. wait for any synchronization status message. press f9 when you want to synchronize all shared notebooks. check whether another device/web view reflects the updated page when practical. what should happen: onenote attempts to synchronize changes. if that does not happen: if sync fails, check internet access, microsoft account sign-in, storage, permissions, and any notebook sync error message. practice: create a harmless test note and force a sync. offline behavior: onenote can cache notes locally, but cloud collaboration depends on later synchronization. avoid assuming another person has seen a change until sync completes. part 18 - accessibility checker and accessible notebook design give notebooks, section groups, sections, and pages unique descriptive names. remove unused empty pages/sections that create navigation noise. add alt text to meaningful pictures and embedded files. use meaningful hyperlink text. do not use color alone to convey meaning. use readable contrast and formatting. keep tables simple. prefer one predictable vertical reading order rather than scattering many note containers around the canvas. run accessibility checker before sharing important notebook content. use immersive reader as an additional way to review how note text flows. 18.1 run accessibility checker what you will learn: find common barriers before sharing. before you begin: open a representative page/notebook. exactly how to do it open review or the accessibility controls available in your current onenote version. choose check accessibility. move through issues in the accessibility pane. read why each issue matters. correct missing alt text, vague page names, poor links, or other issues. recheck. what should happen: the notebook has fewer accessibility barriers. if that does not happen: if accessibility checker is unavailable in the current view/device, open the notebook in the full desktop or web onenote version where microsoft provides the checker. practice: fix at least two practice issues. part 19 - narrator with onenote task command start/stop narrator windows+ctrl+enter narrator input learning narrator+1 next/previous item narrator+right/left arrow primary action narrator+enter 19.1 navigate onenote with narrator what you will learn: use onenote focus shortcuts while narrator announces context. before you begin: narrator is on and onenote is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g and choose a notebook. press ctrl+shift+g and choose a section. press ctrl+alt+g and choose a page. press tab into page content. use narrator reading commands as needed. use ctrl+shift+t to return to the page title. what should happen: narrator follows the notebook hierarchy and page content. if that does not happen: if narrator begins moving through unrelated ribbon controls, use the onenote focus shortcuts to reestablish location. practice: navigate notebook > section > page > content. part 20 - nvda with onenote 20.1 navigate and review with nvda what you will learn: use standard onenote focus while nvda reports controls/text. before you begin: nvda is running. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g to choose a notebook. press ctrl+shift+g for sections. press ctrl+alt+g for pages. press nvda+tab when you want nvda to repeat the focused control/item. press tab into the content area and edit normally. use nvda+f to inspect formatting when useful. what should happen: nvda follows onenote focus and editing. if that does not happen: if nvda reports the ribbon when you expect page text, return to pages/content with ctrl+alt+g and tab. practice: navigate and edit one practice page. part 21 - jaws with onenote 21.1 navigate onenote with jaws what you will learn: use onenote structure while jaws provides speech/help. before you begin: jaws is running. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g for notebooks. press ctrl+shift+g for sections. press ctrl+alt+g for pages. press insert+tab to repeat the focused item when needed. press tab into the page content. use insert+h or command search when you need jaws help. what should happen: jaws follows onenote hierarchy and page content. if that does not happen: if a jaws command conflicts with onenote, use jaws help and onenote's official shortcut list rather than guessing. practice: navigate through two notebooks and several pages. part 22 - voiceover and onenote for mac onenote for mac uses different shortcuts and voiceover interaction patterns. microsoft documents voiceover-compatible navigation for the mac app. use voiceover interaction commands to enter notebook, section, page, and content areas. microsoft documents command+control+g to move keyboard focus to the page list. microsoft documents control+shift+g to move keyboard focus to the section list. use command+s to synchronize the current notebook and command+shift+s to synchronize all notebooks. use voiceover's vo+tab pass-through when a onenote shortcut conflicts with a voiceover command. practice: on mac, identify notebook, section, page list, page title, and content using voiceover before relying on memorized windows commands. part 23 - onenote for the web onenote for the web runs inside a browser. microsoft recommends microsoft edge for the web version and notes that browser-based shortcuts differ from the desktop app. use ctrl+f6 rather than desktop f6 to move among web application command regions. narrator is tested in microsoft edge; jaws and nvda are also tested in chrome in microsoft's accessibility documentation. browser shortcuts such as ctrl+o and f1 apply to the browser rather than the onenote desktop app. use the web version when you need access from a computer without the desktop onenote app. expect some advanced features to be simplified compared with desktop onenote. part 24 - braille displays braille output and input are provided through narrator, nvda, jaws, or voiceover. onenote exposes the notebook hierarchy, page text, tags, links, and controls to the screen reader. 24.1 test braille with onenote what you will learn: verify output, input, and routing. before you begin: configure the braille display in the active screen reader. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g and read notebook names in braille. press ctrl+shift+g and read section names. press ctrl+alt+g and read page titles. open a page and tab into its content. type a short note using braille input if supported. use a routing key inside the text if supported. what should happen: braille follows onenote focus and page editing. if that does not happen: if braille works in other apps but not onenote, verify onenote focus before changing braille settings. practice: test notebook, section, page, text input, and routing. part 25 - iphone/ipad and android 25.1 iphone/ipad with voiceover swipe right/left to move voiceover focus; double-tap to activate. onenote organizes notebooks into sections and pages; voiceover may announce page note containers as content blocks. use the notebooks/recent notes areas to find content quickly. use the voiceover rotor for efficient text and control navigation. test sharing and deletion commands carefully because mobile menus can change with app updates. 25.2 android with talkback swipe right/left to move talkback focus; double-tap to activate. use the notebook, section, and page lists to move through the hierarchy. use standard talkback text-editing gestures/keyboard commands in page content. microsoft recommends using the built-in talkback screen reader as one way to review notebook navigation order. part 26 - security and privacy onenote notebooks can contain highly sensitive information such as meeting notes, passwords copied by mistake, client/student information, or recordings. do not store passwords or authentication codes in ordinary notebook pages unless an approved secure process explicitly permits it. before sharing a notebook, inspect all sections—not only the page you intend the recipient to read. password-protected sections are not a substitute for organization-wide information-security policy. audio notes can record other people; follow consent and local/legal/workplace requirements. synced notebooks may exist on multiple devices and cloud services. delete or move sensitive content only when you understand how sync affects the cloud and collaborators. password-protected sections: microsoft documents ctrl+alt+l to lock all password-protected sections. remember that forgotten onenote section passwords generally cannot simply be recovered by microsoft. part 27 - troubleshooting 27.1 you are typing in the wrong place what you will learn: return to the intended page content area. before you begin: onenote is open. exactly how to do it press escape to close menus/dialogs. press ctrl+alt+g and select the intended page. press tab once to enter page content. type one test character. undo with ctrl+z. what should happen: typing occurs on the intended page. if that does not happen: if focus remains on the title, press tab again. practice: practice recovering from the page list. 27.2 you cannot find a page what you will learn: search rather than scanning every section. before you begin: know one distinctive word or phrase. exactly how to do it press ctrl+e. type the search term. review results. open the matching page. if you only need the current page, use ctrl+f instead. what should happen: you locate the note through search. if that does not happen: if results are stale, force sync and search again. practice: find one page by text rather than page title. 27.3 sync is stuck what you will learn: separate network/account problems from note-editing problems. before you begin: a cloud notebook is not updating. exactly how to do it press shift+f9. listen for sync status/errors. verify internet access. verify the correct microsoft account is signed in. check whether the notebook is stored in onedrive/sharepoint and you still have permission. resolve any named sync conflict/error before creating duplicate notebooks. what should happen: the cause becomes clearer or sync resumes. if that does not happen: avoid repeatedly copying the whole notebook as a troubleshooting step; this can create conflicting versions. practice: force sync and inspect status. 27.4 a page or section moved unexpectedly what you will learn: use hierarchy shortcuts to reestablish location. before you begin: you feel lost after reorganizing. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g and confirm the notebook. press ctrl+shift+g and review sections/section groups. press ctrl+alt+g and review pages. use ctrl+e search if the item still cannot be found. what should happen: you rebuild notebook context and find the item. if that does not happen: if another collaborator moved content, check shared-notebook activity/version information where available. practice: practice recovering after moving a practice page. 27.5 content blocks read in a confusing order what you will learn: simplify free-form page layout. before you begin: a page has several scattered note containers. exactly how to do it use ctrl+a three times and tab/shift+tab to inspect content blocks. identify the intended reading sequence. move important text into one main vertical note container where practical. use headings/lists instead of visual spatial placement to express structure. run accessibility checker again. what should happen: the page becomes more predictable for screen-reader reading. if that does not happen: free-form spatial layouts can be visually useful but harder for assistive technology; prioritize logical order on shared accessible pages. practice: simplify one practice page. part 28 - independent practice course level 1 - orientation ☐ open onenote. ☐ identify notebook. ☐ identify section. ☐ identify page. ☐ enter page content. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 2 - create structure ☐ create section. ☐ create two pages. ☐ rename a page. ☐ move among pages. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 3 - editing ☐ type notes. ☐ correct errors. ☐ bold/italicize text. ☐ undo/redo. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 4 - lists and tags ☐ create bullet list. ☐ create numbered list. ☐ create two-level outline. ☐ apply to do and important tags. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 5 - tables and links ☐ create simple table. ☐ insert descriptive link. ☐ add image alt text. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 6 - search ☐ search current page. ☐ search all notebooks. ☐ open search result. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 7 - organization ☐ move page. ☐ move section. ☐ create section group. ☐ move section into group. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 8 - sharing and sync ☐ inspect share. ☐ force current-notebook sync. ☐ force all-notebook sync. ☐ explain notebook-level privacy risk. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 9 - accessibility ☐ use descriptive names. ☐ simplify content blocks. ☐ run accessibility checker. ☐ fix two issues. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 10 - screen reader ☐ navigate with narrator/nvda/jaws. ☐ use screen-reader help. ☐ recover from wrong focus. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 11 - braille ☐ read notebook/section/page names. ☐ type note. ☐ use routing if supported. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 12 - independent notebook ☐ create a practice notebook structure with sections/pages. ☐ add list/table/link/image/tag. ☐ search it. ☐ sync it. ☐ inspect sharing and accessibility. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. part 29 - quick reference commands navigation and organization - windows desktop task command notebook picker ctrl+g sections pane ctrl+shift+g pages pane ctrl+alt+g new section ctrl+t new page ctrl+n page title ctrl+shift+t search all notebooks ctrl+e search current page ctrl+f move selected page/section up shift+alt+up move selected page/section down shift+alt+down sync all shared notebooks f9 sync current shared notebook shift+f9 lock password-protected sections ctrl+alt+l formatting and notes task command bold / italic / underline ctrl+b / ctrl+i / ctrl+u bulleted list ctrl+period numbered list ctrl+/ or ctrl+shift+o move paragraph up/down alt+shift+up / alt+shift+down indent/outdent paragraph alt+shift+right / alt+shift+left to do / important / question tags ctrl+1 / ctrl+2 / ctrl+3 remove note tags ctrl+0 start audio recording ctrl+alt+a play selected audio ctrl+alt+p stop audio playback ctrl+alt+s screen reader reminders task command narrator input learning narrator+1 nvda input help nvda+1 jaws keyboard help insert+1 voiceover keyboard help vo+k part 30 - official microsoft resources screen reader support for onenote explore and navigate onenote with a screen reader keyboard shortcuts in onenote basic tasks using a screen reader with onenote organize notebooks, sections, and pages with a screen reader share and collaborate on notebooks with a screen reader make onenote notebooks accessible accessibility tools for onenote search notes in onenote final independence checklist ☐ i understand notebook, section, section group, page, page title, and content block. ☐ i can switch notebooks, sections, and pages by keyboard. ☐ i can create and rename sections and pages. ☐ i can type, edit, format, undo, and redo notes. ☐ i can create lists, outlines, tags, and simple tables. ☐ i can insert descriptive links and alt text. ☐ i can search the current page and all notebooks. ☐ i understand onenote audio-note controls and privacy. ☐ i can move, copy, rename, and delete practice pages/sections. ☐ i can create and use section groups. ☐ i can inspect notebook sharing and collaboration. ☐ i can force synchronization and understand offline behavior. ☐ i can run accessibility checker and improve note structure. ☐ i can use onenote with narrator, nvda, jaws, or voiceover. ☐ i can use onenote for the web when needed. ☐ i can use a braille display with onenote. ☐ i understand onenote security/privacy risks. ☐ i can troubleshoot focus, search, sync, hierarchy, and content-block order. most important habit: when you get lost in onenote, rebuild the hierarchy in order: ctrl+g for notebook, ctrl+shift+g for section, ctrl+alt+g for page, then tab into page content. that sequence solves many orientation problems without changing settings. return to all manuals

entries.title: Microsoft Outlook Manual
entries.snippet: Microsoft Outlook Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft outlook manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft outlook manual email, calendar, contacts, narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft outlook accessibility support purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning microsoft outlook. it assumes little or no prior outlook experience and explains exactly what to press, what should happen, and how to recover if the result is different. current interface: this manual uses new outlook for windows as its primary reference. microsoft still supports other outlook versions, so some controls and shortcuts differ in classic outlook, outlook on the web, mac, ios, and android. screen readers: microsoft documents new outlook with narrator, jaws, and nvda. the windows keyboard steps in this manual work regardless of screen reader, while screen-reader-specific notes are labeled separately. how to use this manual work through parts 1-12 first if outlook is completely new to you. do one action at a time and listen to the result before pressing another key. tab moves forward through controls; shift+tab moves backward. arrow keys move within lists, menus, and message lists. enter opens the selected message, event, link, or control. escape closes menus, dialogs, or reading panes in many contexts. ctrl+f6 moves between major outlook regions in new outlook and outlook on the web. microsoft recommends turning the reading pane off for some screen-reader workflows because it simplifies focus movement. when a command differs between new outlook and classic outlook, this manual prioritizes new outlook and labels classic behavior separately where useful. table of contents one application. new outlook for windows has a modern interface similar to outlook on the web. mail contains your inbox, folders, sent items, drafts, junk, deleted items, and other mail folders. calendar contains appointments, meetings, and online-meeting links. people/contacts stores contact information when available. search finds messages, people, events, and other outlook content. the folder/message list and reading/composition areas are separate regions of the interface. part 2 - open outlook and identify your version 2.1 open outlook from windows search what you will learn: launch outlook without a mouse. before you begin: outlook must be installed or provisioned for your account. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type outlook. use up/down arrow if more than one outlook result appears. press enter on outlook. wait for the outlook window to load. if sign-in is requested, follow your organization or microsoft account sign-in process. what should happen: outlook opens to mail or the last-used outlook module. if that does not happen: if outlook does not appear in windows search, use outlook on the web or contact your organization about installation. practice: close and reopen outlook once. 2.2 identify new outlook vs classic outlook what you will learn: know which instructions apply to your interface. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it use tab or ctrl+f6 to move through major interface regions. listen for a command such as try the new outlook if you are in classic outlook. if you hear command toolbar and do not hear try the new outlook, you are likely already using the newer outlook experience. you can also inspect outlook help/about if your organization allows it. what should happen: you know whether you are using new or classic outlook. if that does not happen: if you are unsure, use microsoft's what version of outlook do i have guidance or compare the current interface with your organization documentation. practice: identify the version before learning many shortcuts. part 3 - learn the outlook window app/navigation area: switches among mail, calendar, people, and other microsoft 365 apps. folder pane: inbox, sent items, drafts, deleted items, junk email, and custom folders. message list: shows messages in the selected folder. reading pane: can show the selected message without opening a separate window. command toolbar/ribbon: new mail, delete, archive, move, flag, and other commands. search: finds mail, contacts, and calendar items. 3.1 explore the window with ctrl+f6 what you will learn: move among major outlook regions efficiently. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f6 once. listen to the region name. press ctrl+f6 again. continue cycling through the major outlook regions. within a region, use tab, shift+tab, and arrow keys. press escape if you enter a temporary menu or dialog. what should happen: focus cycles through major outlook landmarks/regions. if that does not happen: if ctrl+f6 behaves differently, verify that outlook rather than your browser has focus. in outlook on the web, ctrl+f6 is also the expected region-navigation key. practice: cycle through all major regions twice. part 4 - essential keyboard navigation task command new email ctrl+n reply ctrl+r reply all ctrl+shift+r forward ctrl+f send ctrl+enter search ctrl+e calendar ctrl+2 mail ctrl+1 move among major regions ctrl+f6 mark read ctrl+q mark unread ctrl+u delete selected message delete important: shortcut behavior can vary between new outlook, classic outlook, and outlook on the web. if a shortcut differs, check microsoft's current keyboard-shortcut page linked at the end of this manual. part 5 - mail: open the inbox and read messages 5.1 open the inbox and move through messages what you will learn: read messages from the message list. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+1 to move to mail. use ctrl+f6 until the folder pane or message list is reached. if focus is in the folder pane, use up/down arrow until inbox is selected and press enter if needed. move to the message list with tab or ctrl+f6. press up/down arrow through messages. listen to sender, subject, date/time, read/unread status, attachment status, and flag information when your screen reader announces it. press enter to open the selected message. read the message using your screen reader's normal reading commands. press escape to return to the message list when appropriate. what should happen: you can choose a message, open it, read it, and return to the list. if that does not happen: if enter moves focus into a reading pane rather than a separate message, use ctrl+f6/tab to locate message content or turn the reading pane off in settings for a simpler screen-reader workflow. practice: read three messages and return to the inbox list after each one. 5.2 read unread messages efficiently what you will learn: identify messages that still need attention. before you begin: you are in the inbox message list. exactly how to do it use up/down arrow through messages. listen for read/unread status. open an unread message with enter. read the message. return to the message list. if needed, mark a message unread again with ctrl+u so you can return to it later. what should happen: you can distinguish read from unread mail and control the status. if that does not happen: if your screen reader does not announce read/unread status, review verbosity settings or use ctrl+q/ctrl+u deliberately and confirm the new state. practice: mark one practice message unread, then read again. part 6 - create and send a new email 6.1 write and send a basic email what you will learn: create a new message from the keyboard. before you begin: know the recipient address and subject. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n. outlook should place focus in the to field. type the recipient name or email address. if suggestions appear, use down arrow through suggestions and press enter on the correct recipient. press tab to move through cc/bcc or other fields until subject is reached. type a clear subject. press tab until the message body is focused. type your message. review the message before sending. press ctrl+enter to send. if outlook asks for send confirmation, read the prompt and confirm only if the recipient and content are correct. what should happen: the message leaves the compose window and is sent. if that does not happen: if ctrl+enter does not send, use tab to reach the send button and press enter. check whether your organization has disabled the ctrl+enter send shortcut. practice: send a test message to yourself. 6.2 add cc or bcc what you will learn: send copies appropriately. before you begin: a new email is open. exactly how to do it move to the cc or bcc control using tab. activate cc or bcc if the field is hidden. type the recipient name/email. use down arrow through suggestions and enter on the correct person. continue to subject and message body. what should happen: the copied recipient appears in the intended cc or bcc field. if that does not happen: if the field is not visible, look for an option/button to show cc/bcc or use the command toolbar. practice: create a draft with one to and one cc recipient, then discard the draft. part 7 - reply, reply all, and forward 7.1 reply to one sender what you will learn: respond only to the sender. before you begin: a message is open or selected in the message list. exactly how to do it press ctrl+r. type your reply in the message body. review the recipient and text. press ctrl+enter to send. what should happen: your reply is sent to the original sender. if that does not happen: if you intended to include everyone, cancel and use ctrl+shift+r instead. practice: reply to a test message from yourself. 7.2 reply to all what you will learn: respond to all intended recipients. before you begin: a message with multiple recipients is open or selected. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+r. review the to and cc recipient list carefully. remove anyone who should not receive the response. type your reply. press ctrl+enter to send. what should happen: the message is sent to the remaining recipients. if that does not happen: if the recipient list is large or sensitive, review each address before sending. practice: open a multi-recipient message and identify who would receive reply all without actually sending. 7.3 forward an email what you will learn: send the original message to a new person. before you begin: a message is open or selected. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. type the new recipient name/email. use down arrow and enter to resolve the correct recipient. tab to the message body. type a short explanation above the forwarded content if appropriate. press ctrl+enter to send. what should happen: the original message is forwarded to the new recipient. if that does not happen: if ctrl+f opens browser find instead, you may be using outlook on the web with browser focus or a different shortcut profile; use the forward button/command. practice: forward a non-sensitive test message to yourself. part 8 - attach files and open attachments 8.1 attach a file to a new message what you will learn: send a file with email. before you begin: know where the file is saved. exactly how to do it create a new message with ctrl+n. complete to and subject. use tab through compose controls until attach/attach file is focused, or open the command toolbar attachment control. press enter. choose browse this computer, onedrive, or another available source. use the file picker to locate the file. press enter on the file. wait for the attachment to finish uploading/attaching. review the attachment name before sending. press ctrl+enter to send. what should happen: the file appears as an attachment and sends with the message. if that does not happen: if attachment fails, check file size, permissions, network connection, and organizational policy. practice: attach a harmless text file to a draft and remove it before discarding. 8.2 open or save an attachment what you will learn: access a file someone sent to you. before you begin: open an email containing an attachment. exactly how to do it use tab or screen-reader navigation until the attachment is focused. press enter to open the attachment menu or file. choose preview/open if you only need to read it. choose download/save as if you need a local copy. if saving, use the windows file picker to choose a folder and confirm save. scan or verify unexpected attachments before opening when security is uncertain. what should happen: the attachment opens or is saved to the chosen location. if that does not happen: if the attachment is blocked, outlook or your organization may consider the file type unsafe. practice: save a safe attachment from a test message. part 9 - search for email 9.1 search by sender, subject, or keyword what you will learn: find a message without browsing every folder. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+e. type a sender name, email address, subject phrase, or distinctive keyword. wait for results. use tab and arrow keys to move through filters/results. open the desired result with enter. press escape or clear the search to return to the normal folder view. what should happen: search results narrow to matching mail. if that does not happen: if there are too many results, add another keyword, sender, or date-related filter. practice: find a message from a known sender using search. part 10 - organize the inbox ctrl+q marks the selected message read. ctrl+u marks it unread. flag marks a message for follow-up. archive removes a message from inbox without deleting it. move places a message in another folder. rules/filters can automate organization if your account permits them. 10.1 mark read or unread what you will learn: control whether a message still appears as needing attention. before you begin: select a message in the message list. exactly how to do it press ctrl+q to mark it read. listen for the status change. press ctrl+u to mark it unread. listen for the status change again. what should happen: the message read/unread state changes. if that does not happen: if there is no audible confirmation, move away and back or inspect the status with your screen reader. practice: toggle one practice message read and unread. 10.2 archive a message what you will learn: remove mail from inbox without deleting it. before you begin: select a non-important practice message. exactly how to do it move to archive using the command toolbar or current shortcut if configured. activate archive. confirm the message disappears from inbox. open the archive folder and locate the message if you want to verify it. what should happen: the message is stored in archive rather than deleted items. if that does not happen: if the account has no archive folder, use move to place the message in another folder. practice: archive a test message and find it again. part 11 - folders and moving messages 11.1 open a mail folder what you will learn: move among inbox, sent, drafts, junk, deleted, and custom folders. before you begin: outlook is in mail. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f6 until the folder pane is focused. use up/down arrow through folders. expand a folder tree with right arrow if needed. press enter on the desired folder. move to the message list with ctrl+f6 or tab. what should happen: the selected folder's message list is displayed. if that does not happen: if a folder is collapsed, expand the parent account/folder with right arrow. practice: open sent items and return to inbox. 11.2 move a message to another folder what you will learn: organize mail into a chosen folder. before you begin: select a practice message. exactly how to do it open the move command from the command toolbar or context menu. use arrow keys/search to locate the destination folder. press enter on the destination. open that folder to verify the message moved. what should happen: the message leaves the original folder and appears in the destination. if that does not happen: if the message remains, you may have copied rather than moved it; inspect the move menu choice. practice: move a test message to a practice folder and move it back. part 12 - delete, archive, flag, mark read/unread 12.1 delete a message safely what you will learn: move unwanted mail to deleted items. before you begin: select a non-important message. exactly how to do it read the sender and subject to confirm selection. press delete. confirm it disappears from the current folder. open deleted items if you need to restore it. what should happen: the message moves to deleted items. if that does not happen: if you deleted the wrong message, open deleted items promptly and move/restore it. practice: delete and restore a practice message. part 13 - junk, phishing, and safe email habits do not open unexpected attachments simply because they appear to come from someone you know. check the actual sender address, not just the display name. be cautious with urgent requests for passwords, gift cards, money, login codes, or account verification. do not enter a password after following an unexpected email link unless you independently verify the site. use outlook's report phishing/junk controls when appropriate and allowed by your organization. when uncertain, contact the sender through a separate known method. accessibility tip: screen-reader users should navigate to the actual link destination when possible instead of trusting only the visible link text. part 14 - contacts and people 14.1 find a contact what you will learn: search the people/contacts area. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it open people/contacts from the outlook app/navigation area. through available phone, email, organization, and contact actions. what should happen: the contact card/details open. if that does not happen: if the person is not saved, outlook may still show directory results from your organization. practice: find one known contact and return to mail. part 15 - calendar basics 15.1 open calendar what you will learn: move from mail to calendar. before you ctrl+1/ctrl+2. 15.2 change calendar view what you will learn: choose a useful day/week/month view. before you begin: calendar is open. exactly how to do it press tab or shift+tab until the view controls are reached. use right/left arrow through day, work week, week, month, or available view choices. press enter on the desired view. in current new outlook, alt+1 through alt+7 can show a selected number of days starting from today where supported. what should happen: the calendar changes to the selected view. if that does not happen: if shortcut behavior differs, use the view buttons on the calendar toolbar. practice: switch between day and week/month views. part 16 - open and navigate calendar events 16.1 browse events what you will learn: move among events in the current open. exactly how to do it move to new event and press enter. type the event title. tab through date and start/end time controls and enter/select the correct values. add a location if needed. add notes/details. set reminder time if desired. review recurrence if it repeats. move to save and press enter. what should happen: the event appears on your calendar. if that does not happen: if save is unavailable, check required date/time fields. practice: create a 15-minute practice appointment and delete it later. part 18 - schedule a meeting and invite people 18.1 create a meeting invitation what you will learn: schedule an event that includes attendees. before you begin: calendar is open and you know the attendee names/emails. exactly how to do it open new event. type the meeting title. move to invite attendees. type the first person's name/email. use down arrow through suggestions and press enter on the correct person. repeat for additional attendees. set the date and start/end times. add a physical location or online meeting option if needed. type an agenda or instructions in the details/body. review attendees and time carefully. move to send and press enter. what should happen: invitations are sent and the meeting appears on your calendar. if that does not happen: if a person does not resolve, verify spelling/email or choose the correct directory suggestion. practice: create a practice meeting with yourself or a safe test account. part 19 - respond to meeting invitations 19.1 accept, tentative, or decline what you will learn: respond to an invitation deliberately. before you begin: open a meeting request email or calendar invitation. exactly how to do it read the organizer, title, date, time, and location/online information. move to accept, tentative, or decline. choose the response that matches your availability. if outlook asks whether to send a response, choose the appropriate option. check calendar to confirm the event status. what should happen: the organizer receives your response when sent, and calendar reflects your choice. if that does not happen: if the event conflicts with another appointment, open calendar before responding to compare times. practice: open a test invitation and identify all three response options. part 20 - join teams/online meetings from outlook 20.1 join an online meeting from calendar what you will learn: use outlook calendar to launch teams or another online meeting. before you begin: the event contains an online meeting link. exactly how to do it press ctrl+2 to open calendar. navigate to the meeting. open it with enter. tab through details until join/join online meeting is focused. press enter. allow teams/browser/meeting app to open. complete microphone, camera, and join options in the meeting application. what should happen: the meeting application opens to the correct meeting. if that does not happen: if join is missing, the event may not contain online meeting details or you may be opening an outdated occurrence. practice: open a future online meeting and locate join without joining. part 21 - recurring meetings 21.1 create a recurring event what you will learn: schedule repeated events without creating each one manually. before you begin: create a new calendar event. exactly how to do it enter title, attendees if needed, and first date/time. move to repeat/recurrence. choose daily, weekly, monthly, or a custom recurrence pattern. set an end date or occurrence limit if appropriate. review the recurrence summary. save/send. what should happen: outlook creates the repeating series. if that does not happen: if the recurrence is wrong, edit the series before many invitations/occurrences are created. practice: create a weekly practice event calendar is open. exactly how to do it move to search using ctrl+e or the search box. type part of the event title, organizer, or keyword. review results with arrows/tab. press enter on the desired event. what should happen: the matching event opens or is highlighted. if that does not happen: if search returns mail too, refine the query or use calendar-specific search/filter controls. practice: and windows notification behavior. 23.1 change an event reminder what you will learn: control how early outlook reminds you. before you begin: open an event you created. exactly how to do it tab to the reminder control. open the list. choose the desired time, such as 5 minutes, 15 minutes, 1 hour, or another available value. save the event. what should happen: the event stores the selected reminder time. if that does not happen: if no reminder is available, check whether the event type/account supports reminders. practice: change a practice appointment reminder and restore it. part 24 - settings and accessibility 24.1 open outlook settings what you will learn: change outlook preferences carefully. before you begin: outlook is open. exactly how to do it move to settings using the gear/settings control or its current shortcut if assigned. use tab/arrow navigation through settings categories. find mail, calendar, general, accessibility, or related sections. change only one setting at a time. close settings and test the result. what should happen: outlook uses the changed setting. if that does not happen: if you cannot find a setting in new outlook, it may be in the outlook web settings or unavailable under organization policy. practice: find reading pane and notification settings without changing them. screen-reader recommendation: microsoft accessibility guidance notes that turning the reading pane off and showing emails as messages rather than conversations can simplify some screen-reader workflows. part 25 - spell check, formatting, and accessible email 25.1 review spelling and grammar what you will learn: correct obvious writing errors before sending. before you begin: a draft message contains text. exactly how to do it use outlook's editor/spelling and grammar controls or the current shortcut for spelling review. move through each suggested issue. listen to the flagged word and suggested corrections. accept a correction only when it matches your intended meaning. ignore false positives when appropriate. return to the message and review before sending. what should happen: the draft contains the intended corrections. if that does not happen: if editor does not open, check whether your account/version has microsoft editor enabled. practice: create a draft with one spelling error and correct it. use meaningful subject lines. use descriptive link text rather than “click here.” use headings and lists in long messages when helpful. add alt text to meaningful images when the compose tools provide it. do not communicate reply. type the reply. if virtual cursor/forms behavior interferes, use jaws application help with insert+h or command search. press ctrl+enter to send. what should happen: jaws reads the message and navigate outlook mail basic calendar tasks with a screen reader explore and navigate outlook calendar organize your inbox in new outlook check spelling and grammar with a screen reader final independence checklist ☐ i can open outlook and identify new vs classic outlook. ☐ i can move among major outlook regions. ☐ i can read, create, reply to, forward, and send mail. ☐ i can search and organize my inbox. ☐ i can use folders, archive, delete, and mark read/unread. ☐ i can attach and save files safely. ☐ i can identify suspicious email and phishing warning signs. ☐ i can use outlook calendar. ☐ i can create appointments and meetings. ☐ i can respond to invitations and join online meetings. ☐ i can use outlook with narrator, nvda, or jaws as appropriate. ☐ i can recover when focus or reading mode becomes confusing. ☐ i know where to find microsoft's current outlook accessibility documentation. most important habit: before sending, deleting, moving, or responding, stop and confirm the selected message, recipients, and action. outlook is fastest when you combine keyboard shortcuts with deliberate confirmation. return to all manuals

entries.title: Microsoft PowerPoint Accessible Manual
entries.snippet: Accessible Microsoft PowerPoint manual for Microsoft 365 desktop on Windows with JAWS and keyboard-first instruction.
entries.text: microsoft powerpoint manual - accessible learning center keyboard-first microsoft 365 training microsoft powerpoint accessible manual create, review, and present accessible slide decks with jaws and the keyboard. keyboard quick reference accessible slide practices course lessons about this manual this manual targets powerpoint in microsoft 365 desktop on windows. powerpoint contains several work areas, including the thumbnails pane, slide editing area, notes pane, and ribbon. press f6 to move among these areas and tab or shift+tab to move among objects on a slide. use built-in slide layouts whenever possible. layout placeholders provide structure that is easier to navigate and maintain than manually positioned text boxes. give every slide a unique, descriptive title. keyboard quick reference common powerpoint commands used in this course task command move among powerpoint panes f6 or shift+f6 move among slide objects tab or shift+tab create a new slide ctrl+m duplicate a selected slide or object ctrl+d move to next or previous slide in thumbnails down arrow or up arrow edit text in a selected placeholder enter or f2 exit text editing and select the object escape insert or edit a hyperlink ctrl+k save ctrl+s save as f12 start slide show from beginning f5 start slide show from current slide shift+f5 advance during slide show right arrow, spacebar, or page down move backward during slide show left arrow, backspace, or page up end slide show escape temporarily show a black screen b search office commands alt+q search jaws commands insert+spacebar, then j accessible slide practices use built-in slide layouts and give every slide a unique title. keep text concise and use real bulleted or numbered lists. maintain strong contrast and do not use color as the only way to communicate meaning. add concise alternative text to meaningful pictures, charts, shapes, and other visual objects. mark objects decorative only when they add no information. use the reading order pane to arrange objects logically, with the title before related content. use simple tables with a designated header row. avoid merged or split cells. for charts, retain source values and add a plain-text summary of the important result. use meaningful link text that identifies the destination. add speaker-note prompts to describe visuals aloud during a presentation. avoid flashing content and unnecessary animation. run check accessibility and test the entire deck with the keyboard. reading order screen readers follow the slide's object order, which may differ from the visual arrangement. open the reading order pane through alt+q or an accessibility checker recommendation, then move objects into a logical sequence. test that sequence by pressing tab through the slide. images, tables, and charts alt text should explain why a visual matters in the presentation. it should be concise, specific, and based on the presentation context. a chart needs alt text plus access to exact source values and a short text summary. a table needs clear headers and a simple structure. presenting accessibly start the slide show with f5, move with the arrow keys, and press escape to finish. speak important information shown in images, charts, and demonstrations. do not ask the audience to identify information only by color, position, or appearance. ten-lesson course sequence lesson 1: powerpoint basics: slides, placeholders, and saving — create a basic presentation, move among slide placeholders with the keyboard, and save the file. lesson 2: slide layouts, titles, and organizing a presentation — use built-in slide layouts and meaningful titles to create a clear presentation structure. lesson 3: text, bullets, and clear slide content — create concise, structured slide text that works for screen-reader users and visual audiences. lesson 4: images, alternative text, and decorative objects — insert an image and make its meaning available to people who cannot see it. lesson 5: reading order and keyboard navigation — arrange slide objects so a screen reader encounters them in a logical order. lesson 6: accessible tables and charts — present structured data with clear headers, accessible descriptions, and a text summary. lesson 7: meaningful links and contact information — add links that clearly identify their destination and work with keyboard navigation. lesson 8: color, contrast, fonts, and accessible design — apply a professional design that remains readable with low vision and does not communicate by color alone. lesson 9: speaker notes and presenting with the keyboard — prepare concise speaker notes and deliver a presentation using keyboard commands. lesson 10: final accessible workplace presentation — independently create, check, and practice a professional accessible presentation. begin powerpoint lesson 1 official references and further learning microsoft: create accessible office documents microsoft: making documents accessible microsoft: add alternative text to objects microsoft: accessibility checker freedom scientific: jaws documentation view powerpoint lessons view my progress return to manuals

entries.title: Microsoft Teams Manual
entries.snippet: Microsoft Teams Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft teams manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft teams manual meetings, chat, channels, files, calls, and screen readers independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft teams accessibility support purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning microsoft teams. it assumes you may be using teams for the first time. every procedure explains where to go, what to press or select, what should happen, and what to try if the result is different. important: microsoft teams changes frequently and organizations can customize which apps appear and in what order. if a numbered app shortcut differs from this manual, use the app's current position in your teams app bar or use search/keyboard navigation instead. accessibility focus: the manual includes mouse/visual instructions where useful and detailed keyboard/screen-reader methods for windows and mac. microsoft documents teams with narrator, jaws, nvda, and voiceover. how to use this manual work through parts 1-8 first if you are completely new to teams. do one action at a time. after each action, stop and confirm what changed. tab moves forward through many controls. shift+tab moves backward. enter usually activates the focused button, link, chat, or menu item. spacebar often toggles switches and checkboxes. escape usually closes a menu, returns focus to a list, or backs out of a temporary interface. windows shortcut labels in this manual refer to the teams desktop app unless the section specifically says web. mac shortcuts use command where microsoft documents a mac-specific equivalent. screen-reader users should listen to both the control name and control type before activating it. teams may use combined chats and channels or separate list views. this manual explains both concepts. table of contents part 1 - what microsoft teams is part 2 - install, open, and sign in part 3 - learn the teams window and app bar part 4 - essential keyboard navigation part 5 - search part 6 - chat: find, read, start, and send messages part 7 - chat formatting, attachments, reactions, and mentions part 8 - chats and channels: combined and separate views part 9 - teams and channels part 10 - files part 11 - calendar part 12 - schedule a meeting part 13 - join a meeting part 14 - meeting controls: microphone, camera, people, chat, and leave part 15 - captions, transcription, reactions, raise hand, and accessibility part 16 - share your screen or content part 17 - calls part 18 - activity and notifications part 19 - status, profile, and settings part 20 - audio and video device settings part 21 - screen reader navigation on windows part 22 - voiceover navigation on mac part 23 - teams on the web part 24 - mobile teams basics part 25 - troubleshooting part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference keyboard commands part 28 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what microsoft teams is microsoft teams is a communication and collaboration application. depending on your account and organization, you can use it for individual and group chat, team/channel conversations, meetings, calls, calendar events, file sharing, and connected microsoft 365 apps. chat is usually best for direct or small-group conversations. channels organize ongoing discussions and files around a team, department, class, project, or topic. calendar shows teams meetings and connected microsoft 365 calendar events. meetings include audio/video, participant controls, meeting chat, captions, reactions, and content sharing. calls can be person-to-person or group calls when calling is enabled for your account. files shared through teams may be stored in onedrive or sharepoint depending on where they are shared. terminology: a 'team' is a larger workspace or membership group. a 'channel' is a subject or working area inside a team. a 'chat' is a direct conversation that is not necessarily tied to a channel. part 2 - install, open, and sign in 2.1 open teams on windows what you will learn: open the teams desktop app using the keyboard. before you begin: microsoft teams must already be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type teams. wait for microsoft teams to appear in search results. press enter. wait for the teams window to open. if a sign-in screen appears, move to the account/email field with tab if necessary. type your work, school, or microsoft account email address. press tab until next/sign in is focused and press enter. follow the authentication prompts. type your password, approve a verification request, or choose the required sign-in method. after sign-in, wait for the main teams window to finish loading before pressing additional navigation keys. what should happen: the main teams interface opens and your account is signed in. if that does not happen: if teams does not appear in windows search, it may not be installed or your organization may use the web version. if sign-in fails, confirm the account and authentication method with your organization. practice: close teams, reopen it from windows search, and confirm that you return to the main interface. 2.2 open teams on a mac what you will learn: open the teams desktop app without using the mouse. before you begin: microsoft teams must already be installed. exactly how to do it press command+space to open spotlight. type microsoft teams. press return. wait for teams to open. if a sign-in screen appears, use tab or voiceover navigation to move to the email/account field. type your account email address. activate next/sign in. follow password and verification prompts until teams opens. what should happen: the teams main window opens. if that does not happen: if spotlight does not find teams, check the applications folder or use teams on the web if permitted. practice: quit teams, reopen it from spotlight, and confirm you are signed in. part 3 - learn the teams window and app bar the teams window is divided into regions. exact names and order can vary, but the same ideas are consistent: an app/navigation area, a list area, and a content/conversation area. app bar: gives access to activity, chat, teams/channels, calendar, calls, and other installed apps. list pane: shows chats, channels, meetings, contacts, or other items for the current app. main content pane: shows the selected conversation, channel, calendar, meeting details, or file. top area: includes search and account/settings controls. right-side panes: can open for people, meeting chat, details, or other contextual information. numbered app shortcuts: microsoft notes that app-number shortcuts depend on the sequential position of the app on your app bar. if you or your organization reorder apps, the number changes. 3.1 explore the window with tab what you will learn: learn where focus moves before relying on shortcuts. before you begin: teams is open and no menu/dialog is active. exactly how to do it press tab once. listen to or visually identify the focused control. press tab again and note the next control. continue through several controls. press shift+tab to move backward. when focus enters a list, use up arrow and down arrow to move among list items if teams exposes the list that way. press escape if focus enters a temporary control or pane you want to leave. repeat until you can identify the app/navigation area, current list, and conversation/content area. what should happen: focus moves predictably among teams controls. if that does not happen: if tab seems trapped in one section, press escape once and try tab again. if a list is active, use arrow keys inside the list rather than repeatedly pressing tab. practice: explore for two minutes without activating anything; simply identify controls. part 4 - essential keyboard navigation task windows desktop mac desktop show keyboard shortcuts ctrl+period (.) or alt+/ command+period (.) go to search ctrl+e command+e open settings ctrl+comma (,) command+comma (,) start a new chat ctrl+n command+n go to a specific chat or channel ctrl+g command+g close/return esc esc mute/unmute in meeting ctrl+shift+m command+shift+m turn camera on/off in meeting ctrl+shift+o command+shift+o may vary by current microsoft mapping; use the in-app shortcut list to confirm best habit: press ctrl+period on windows or command+period on mac whenever you are unsure of a teams shortcut. this opens teams' current shortcut list. 4.1 open the shortcut list what you will learn: use teams itself as a current command reference. before you begin: teams is open. exactly how to do it windows: press ctrl+period (.). mac: press command+period (.). wait for the keyboard-shortcuts window/pane to open. use tab, shift+tab, and arrow keys to review categories and commands. press escape to close it. what should happen: the current teams shortcut list appears. if that does not happen: if the shortcut does not open, use settings and more in the upper-right area, then choose keyboard shortcuts. practice: find the current shortcuts for search, new chat, settings, microphone, and camera. part 5 - search 5.1 search for a person, chat, channel, or content what you will learn: use the search box without manually browsing long lists. before you begin: teams is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+e on windows or command+e on mac. type the name, keyword, person, chat, or channel you want. wait for suggestions/results. use down arrow to move through suggestions when available. read or inspect each result before choosing it. press enter on the desired result. if a broader results page opens, use tab and arrow keys to move among result
