categories and items. press escape if you want to cancel the search. what should happen: the selected person, chat, channel, or search result opens. if that does not happen: if the wrong result opens, press escape or return to search and use a more specific phrase such as a full name or distinctive channel name. practice: search for one coworker/contact and one channel. part 6 - chat: find, read, start, and send messages teams may display chats and channels together or separately. microsoft currently describes combined chats and channels as the default experience, but organizations and users can change the view. 6.1 open an existing chat and read it what you will learn: open a conversation and move through its messages. before you begin: teams is open and the chat/chats and channels area is available. exactly how to do it move to the chat or chats and channels app using the app bar, search, or its numbered shortcut if you know its current position. once focus is in the chat list, press up arrow or down arrow to move one conversation at a time. stop when the desired chat is selected. press spacebar to jump to the oldest unread message when that behavior is available, or press enter to move into the conversation/compose area. use up arrow and down arrow to move through messages when focus is in the message list. listen to or read the sender, message text, time/status information, and any attachment/reaction information. press escape to return focus to the chat list. what should happen: you can move between the chat list and messages without losing the conversation. if that does not happen: if enter jumps directly to the compose box when you wanted to read messages, press shift+tab to move toward the messages list or use spacebar from the chat list to jump to unread messages. practice: open a chat with unread messages, read them, and return to the chat list. 6.2 start a new chat what you will learn: create a direct or group conversation. before you begin: know the name or email address of the person you want to message. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n on windows or command+n on mac. focus should move to the recipient/to field. type the person's name or email address. wait for matching suggestions. use down arrow if there is more than one match. press enter/return on the correct person. to create a group chat, add another person using the same method. press tab until focus moves to the message compose box. type your message. press enter on windows or return on mac to send the message. what should happen: the message appears in the conversation and the chat is added to your chat list. if that does not happen: if enter inserts a new line instead of sending, your compose settings or formatting mode may be different. use the send button or teams' current shortcut behavior. practice: start a chat with a safe test contact and send a short greeting. 6.3 reply to a chat quickly what you will learn: move from the chat list to the compose box and back. before you begin: focus is in the chat list. exactly how to do it use up arrow/down arrow to select the chat. press enter to move into that conversation; microsoft documents this as moving focus to the message compose area in the current chats and channels experience. type your reply. press enter to send. press escape to return focus to the chat list. what should happen: the reply is sent and focus returns to the list after escape. if that does not happen: if escape does not return to the list, press it once more or shift+tab until the list is reached. practice: reply to two chats and return to the list after each one. part 7 - chat formatting, attachments, reactions, and mentions 7.1 mention a person with @ what you will learn: notify a specific person inside a chat or channel message. before you begin: be in a message compose box. exactly how to do it type the @ symbol. immediately type the person's name. wait for matching people to appear. use up arrow or down arrow to move through matches. press enter/return on the correct person. continue typing the message. send the message. what should happen: the person's name becomes a mention and the sent message can notify them according to their notification settings. if that does not happen: if no match appears, check the spelling or whether that person is available in the current organization/team. practice: write a draft mention but do not send it until you confirm the correct person. 7.2 attach a file to a chat what you will learn: send a file with a chat message. before you begin: be in a chat and know where the file is stored. exactly how to do it move through the compose controls with tab until you reach the attachment/file control, or use the current attachment command shown in teams. activate it. choose the source, such as a file from your computer or connected microsoft storage. if a file picker opens, use standard windows/macos file navigation to locate the file. select the file and activate open/attach. wait for the file to finish attaching or uploading. add explanatory text in the message box if desired. send the message. what should happen: the attachment appears with the sent message. if that does not happen: if the attachment fails, verify file access, network connection, file size/type restrictions, and organizational sharing policies. practice: attach a non-sensitive practice file to a test chat. part 8 - chats and channels: combined and separate views microsoft's current teams experience can show chats and channels in one combined list or in separate app/list views. do not assume another person's teams looks exactly like yours. combined view: chats and channels appear together in the same primary experience. separate view: chats and channels are divided into different app/list areas. app shortcuts can change when the app bar order changes. use search or ctrl+g/command+g when you know the destination name but not where it is in the list. 8.1 go directly to a chat or channel what you will learn: open a known destination without browsing the entire list. before you begin: know at least part of the chat or channel name. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g on windows or command+g on mac. type the chat or channel name. use down arrow through matches. press enter/return on the correct result. what should happen: the requested chat or channel opens. if that does not happen: if no result appears, use ctrl+e/command+e search instead and enter a broader keyword. practice: open one chat and one channel using go to. part 9 - teams and channels channels are persistent conversation spaces inside a team. depending on your permissions, channels may be standard, private, or shared. 9.1 open a channel and read posts what you will learn: navigate into a channel conversation. before you begin: be in chats and channels or the teams/channels area. exactly how to do it move through the team/channel list with up arrow and down arrow. if a team is collapsed, use the appropriate expand control or right arrow when supported. move to the desired channel. press enter. move into the posts/conversation area with tab or the screen-reader navigation appropriate to your platform. use arrow keys to read posts/messages. move to the reply/compose control to add a response. type the response and send it. what should happen: the channel opens and you can read and contribute to its conversation. if that does not happen: if you cannot access a channel, you may not be a member or the channel may be private/shared with restricted access. practice: open a channel, read three posts, and return to the channel list. part 10 - files files shared in teams can appear in chat, channels, or file tabs. chat files commonly use onedrive; channel files commonly use the team's sharepoint-backed file storage. 10.1 open a file shared in a conversation what you will learn: find and open a file from a chat or channel. before you begin: open the conversation that contains the file. exactly how to do it move through messages until you reach the message containing the file. move focus to the file attachment/link. press enter/return. wait for the file to open in teams, a microsoft 365 viewer/editor, or your browser depending on file type and settings. use the application's normal navigation to read or edit the file. close the file or use teams navigation to return to the conversation. what should happen: the file opens with the permissions available to your account. if that does not happen: if you are denied access, ask the file owner or organization administrator to check permissions rather than repeatedly retrying. practice: open a safe shared document and return to the original conversation. part 11 - calendar calendar is where you review upcoming meetings, open meeting details, respond to invitations, and create new events. 11.1 open calendar and find a meeting what you will learn: reach an upcoming meeting without using a mouse. before you begin: teams is open. exactly how to do it use the calendar app on the app bar. if you know its current sequential position, use the corresponding ctrl+number on windows or command+number on mac. do not assume the number is fixed. microsoft notes it changes if app order changes. once calendar opens, press tab through the calendar toolbar and meeting items. use arrow keys inside calendar grids or lists when teams exposes them. stop on the meeting you want. press enter/return to open meeting details. what should happen: the selected meeting details open. if that does not happen: if you cannot find the meeting by keyboard navigation, press ctrl+e/command+e and search for the meeting title or organizer. practice: open the next scheduled meeting's details, then return to calendar. part 12 - schedule a meeting 12.1 schedule a meeting with keyboard and screen reader what you will learn: create a meeting, invite people, set time/date, and send the invitation. before you begin: know the meeting title, attendees, date, and time. exactly how to do it open calendar from the app bar. tab until you reach the calendar toolbar. move to new event/new meeting and press enter/return. when the new meeting dialog opens, type the meeting title in the add title field. press tab to the invite attendees field. type the first person's name or email address. wait for suggestions, use down arrow to select the correct person, and press enter/return. repeat for additional attendees. press tab through the date fields. open a date picker if needed, then use arrow keys to choose the date and press enter. tab to start time and end time. use the available time controls or type/select the desired times. tab to recurrence if you need a repeating meeting; open it, use arrow keys to choose the pattern, and confirm. if this is a channel meeting, move to add channel, browse the team/channel hierarchy, and select the correct channel. tab to location if needed. leave it blank for an online-only teams meeting unless a physical location is required. tab to the meeting details/description field and type the agenda or instructions. tab until send is focused. press enter/return. what should happen: the event is created and invitations are sent. if that does not happen: if send is unavailable, verify required fields such as title/date/time and that attendee entries are resolved correctly. practice: create a practice meeting for a future date, then open it from calendar. 12.2 start a meet now meeting what you will learn: start an immediate meeting without first creating a normal calendar invitation. before you begin: open calendar. exactly how to do it tab through the calendar toolbar until meet now is focused. press enter. type or edit the meeting name if a name field is shown. tab to the camera toggle and press spacebar if you want to change its state. tab to the audio option and choose the desired audio mode. tab to start meeting/join and press enter. after the meeting starts, use the invite/participants controls if you need to add people. what should happen: the meeting starts and meeting controls become available. if that does not happen: if teams requests microphone/camera permission, grant or deny according to your needs and organizational policy. practice: start a private practice meet now session and locate the leave button without inviting anyone. part 13 - join a meeting 13.1 join from teams calendar what you will learn: join an existing meeting and make deliberate microphone/camera choices before entering. before you begin: the meeting is visible in teams calendar. exactly how to do it open calendar. tab or navigate to the meeting. move to the join button and activate it. on the pre-join screen, move through camera, microphone, speaker/audio, and other available controls. use spacebar to toggle switches such as camera or microphone when focused. confirm the microphone state you want before joining. confirm the camera state you want before joining. move to join now/join the meeting. press enter/return. wait for the meeting to open. if a lobby is used, wait until admitted. what should happen: you enter the meeting with the audio/video state you selected. if that does not happen: if you cannot join, check the meeting time, internet connection, account permissions, and whether the organizer must admit you from a lobby. practice: join a test meeting with microphone muted and camera off. part 14 - meeting controls meeting action windows mac mute/unmute microphone ctrl+shift+m command+shift+m camera on/off ctrl+shift+o use teams' current shortcut list; microsoft documents camera control and its current mapping can be confirmed in-app leave meeting tab to hang up/leave, enter tab to hang up/leave, return/space 14.1 mute and unmute what you will learn: control whether other participants can hear your microphone. before you begin: be inside a teams meeting. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+m on windows or command+shift+m on mac. listen for or visually confirm the microphone state. press the same shortcut again to reverse the state. before speaking, verify that the microphone is unmuted. after speaking, mute again when appropriate. what should happen: the microphone changes between muted and unmuted. if that does not happen: if the shortcut does not respond, tab to the microphone button and activate it. check the shortcut list because keyboard mappings can change. practice: practice toggling twice and identify the final state. 14.2 open the people/participants pane what you will learn: find out who is in the meeting. before you begin: be inside a meeting. exactly how to do it press tab repeatedly until show participants/people is focused. press enter/return. tab until focus reaches the attendees/participants list. use down arrow to move through participant names and statuses. when finished, tab or shift+tab to close right pane. activate close. what should happen: the people pane opens, names can be reviewed, and the pane closes. if that does not happen: if arrow keys do not move among names, first move focus into the participant tree/list using tab. practice: open people, identify two participant names, and close the pane. 14.3 open meeting chat what you will learn: send and read messages while remaining in a meeting. before you begin: be inside a meeting. exactly how to do it tab through meeting controls until show conversation/chat is focused. press enter/return. focus may move to the new-message field. type your message. press enter/return to send. to read existing messages, press shift+tab toward the message list. use up arrow/down arrow or the platform's documented message navigation to read messages. move to close right pane and activate it when finished. what should happen: the meeting chat pane opens, your message sends, and you can read other messages. if that does not happen: if your typed text does not send, move to the send button and activate it. practice: send a short test message and close the chat pane. 14.4 leave a meeting what you will learn: exit intentionally instead of accidentally closing another pane. before you begin: be inside a meeting. exactly how to do it press tab until hang up/leave is focused. confirm that the control is the meeting leave control, not a pane close button. press enter/return. if teams asks whether to leave or end the meeting for everyone and you are the organizer, choose the option you intend. what should happen: you leave the meeting and return to teams. if that does not happen: if you are still in the meeting, locate hang up/leave again and activate it. closing a side pane does not leave the meeting. practice: from a test meeting, find the leave control and exit. part 15 - captions, transcription, reactions, raise hand, and accessibility teams includes accessibility and participation tools whose availability can depend on meeting policy, organizer settings, language, account type, and organization. live captions display spoken words as text during a meeting. transcription can create a written meeting transcript when allowed. raise hand signals that you want to speak. reactions provide nonverbal responses such as applause or agreement. background noise suppression and voice isolation options can improve focus in some environments. meeting chat provides a text-based alternative or supplement to spoken participation. 15.1 turn on live captions what you will learn: display spoken meeting audio as text when captions are available. before you begin: be inside a meeting. exactly how to do it move through the meeting controls to more/more actions. open the menu. use arrow keys to find language and speech or the current captions/transcription option. choose turn on live captions. wait for the caption region to appear. if prompted for spoken language, choose the correct meeting language. to stop captions, return to the same menu and choose the option to turn them off. what should happen: captions appear as people speak. if that does not happen: if the option is missing, captions may be restricted by meeting policy or your account. check with the organizer or administrator. practice: turn captions on in a test meeting and locate the caption area. part 16 - share your screen or content 16.1 share content in a meeting what you will learn: present your screen, window, or other supported content. before you begin: close or hide private information before sharing. exactly how to do it inside the meeting, press tab through controls until share/share content is focused. press enter/return. move through available choices such as screen, window, powerpoint, whiteboard, or other supported options. choose the smallest appropriate sharing scope. prefer a specific window when you do not need to share everything on your desktop. activate the desired item. wait for teams to indicate that sharing has started. navigate to the application/content you are presenting. when finished, return to teams or the sharing toolbar. activate stop sharing. what should happen: other participants can see the content you selected, and sharing stops when you choose stop sharing. if that does not happen: if the share picker is empty or screen sharing fails, check operating-system screen-recording/privacy permissions and organizational meeting policy. practice: practice sharing a non-sensitive window, confirm sharing, then stop. privacy: before sharing your entire screen, close email, messages, password managers, client records, personal notifications, and any other content that should not be visible to meeting participants. part 17 - calls 17.1 start an audio or video call from a contact/chat what you will learn: call a person directly. before you begin: calling must be enabled for your teams account. exactly how to do it open the chat/contact for the person you want to call. confirm that the correct person or group is selected. for a windows audio call, microsoft documents ctrl+shift+c when focus is on the contact/conversation. for a windows video call, microsoft documents ctrl+shift+u when focus is on the contact/conversation. alternatively, tab to the audio call or video call button and activate it. wait for the other person to answer. use the meeting/call microphone and camera controls as needed. to finish, locate hang up and activate it. what should happen: the call starts with the intended person and ends when hang up is activated. if that does not happen: if call controls are unavailable, your account or organization may not have calling enabled. practice: locate the audio-call and video-call controls in a safe test chat without placing an unwanted call. part 18 - activity and notifications activity collects mentions, replies, reactions, and other events. notifications determine which events interrupt or alert you. 18.1 review activity what you will learn: find recent teams events that need your attention. before you begin: teams is open. exactly how to do it open activity from the app bar. move through activity items with up arrow/down arrow or tab as appropriate. read the type of activity, sender, and related conversation. press enter on an item to open the related chat/channel/message. press escape to return to the activity list. what should happen: you can move from an alert to the relevant conversation and back. if that does not happen: if an activity item opens the wrong context, return and confirm the selected item before pressing enter. practice: open one recent activity item and return. 18.2 change notification settings what you will learn: reduce or increase teams alerts. before you begin: teams is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+comma on windows or command+comma on mac to open settings. navigate to notifications and activity or the current notification category. move through notification types one at a time. for each setting, read the current option before changing it. open the option and choose the desired behavior, such as banner/feed/off, where available. close settings when finished. send or receive a test message if possible to verify the new behavior. what should happen: teams notifications follow the changed settings. if that does not happen: if notifications still do not appear, also check windows/macos system notification permissions and focus/do not disturb modes. practice: review chat-message and meeting notification settings without changing anything first. part 19 - status, profile, and settings 19.1 change your presence status what you will learn: set available, busy, do not disturb, away, or another available status. before you begin: teams is open. exactly how to do it move to your profile/account control near the top of teams. activate it. move to the current status option. open the status menu. use arrow keys to select the desired status. press enter/return. if an option to set duration is available and needed, choose how long teams should keep that status. what should happen: your profile shows the selected status. if that does not happen: if the status changes back automatically, teams may be updating presence based on calendar activity, inactivity, or organization policy. practice: set a temporary status and then restore your normal status. part 20 - audio and video device settings 20.1 choose the correct microphone, speaker, and camera what you will learn: make sure teams is using the intended hardware before an important meeting. before you begin: connect the headset, microphone, speakers, and camera you intend to use. exactly how to do it open settings with ctrl+comma on windows or command+comma on mac. navigate to devices or the current device settings category. move to speaker and read the selected device. open the speaker list and choose the desired output device. move to microphone and choose the desired input device. move to camera and choose the desired camera if video is needed. use make a test call or any available test feature if your account provides it. speak and listen for playback or watch the input meter/feedback where available. close settings. what should happen: teams uses the correct speaker, microphone, and camera. if that does not happen: if the device is missing, reconnect it, check operating-system sound/privacy settings, then restart teams if necessary. practice: verify devices before your next meeting rather than waiting until the meeting starts. part 21 - screen reader navigation on windows microsoft currently documents teams with narrator, jaws, and nvda. recent jaws versions may not use the virtual pc cursor in teams by default, so some microsoft procedures distinguish focus navigation from virtual/browse navigation. 21.1 navigate the chats and channels list with a screen reader what you will learn: move efficiently from conversation list to messages and back. before you begin: teams is running with narrator, jaws, or nvda. exactly how to do it open chat/chats and channels using the app bar or its current numbered shortcut. use down arrow to move one conversation at a time. press spacebar on a conversation to jump to its oldest unread message when supported. use down arrow to move through messages. press escape to return to the chat/channel list. to reply quickly, select the conversation in the list and press enter. type the reply in the compose area. press enter to send. press escape to return to the list. what should happen: you can repeatedly move list → messages/compose → list without hunting through the entire teams window. if that does not happen: if arrow keys are being interpreted as browse/virtual navigation rather than focus navigation, adjust the screen reader's browse/focus mode as appropriate for teams. practice: read one chat, reply, return to the list, then open another chat. part 22 - voiceover navigation on mac on mac, teams can be used with voiceover. standard voiceover concepts still apply: vo+right/left moves among accessible items, vo+shift+down interacts with a group, and vo+shift+up stops interacting. task mac command next voiceover item vo+right arrow previous voiceover item vo+left arrow activate selected control vo+space interact with group vo+shift+down arrow stop interacting vo+shift+up arrow teams search command+e teams shortcuts list command+period (.) teams settings command+comma (,) 22.1 read and reply to a teams chat with voiceover what you will learn: use teams without the mouse on mac. before you begin: voiceover is on and teams is open. exactly how to do it use command+e and search for the chat/person if that is easier than browsing the app bar. press return on the correct result. use vo+right arrow to move through the chat interface. when voiceover announces a group containing messages, press vo+shift+down arrow. use vo+right arrow or the list's arrow-key behavior to move among messages. to reach the compose box, stop interacting when needed with vo+shift+up arrow, then continue vo+right arrow until the message field is announced. type the message. press return to send. listen for confirmation/new message state before navigating away. what should happen: the message is sent and you can continue reading the conversation. if that does not happen: if voiceover skips controls inside a group, interact with that group. if you are stuck inside nested content, use vo+shift+up arrow to move outward. practice: open a chat, read the most recent message, and send a short reply. part 23 - teams on the web teams on the web runs inside a browser, so some shortcuts differ from the desktop app. browser shortcuts can also conflict with teams shortcuts. microsoft recommends edge with narrator for teams on the web; chrome or firefox can be used with jaws/nvda. web app navigation may use ctrl+f6 where desktop teams uses f6-style movement. web search can use ctrl+alt+e rather than the desktop ctrl+e. do not assume desktop shortcuts work identically in the browser. use teams' in-app keyboard-shortcuts list for the exact web mapping. browser caution: keys such as f1, ctrl+o, and other common shortcuts may control the browser rather than teams when you are using the web app. part 24 - mobile teams basics on ios and android, teams uses touch gestures and the device's screen reader. microsoft provides platform-specific accessibility procedures. iphone/ipad: voiceover uses swipes to move focus and double-tap to activate. android: talkback uses swipe navigation and double-tap activation. meeting screens still include microphone, camera, join, people, chat, and leave controls, but their location can differ from desktop. for precise mobile screen-reader procedures, use microsoft's current teams accessibility support because mobile layouts change frequently. part 25 - troubleshooting 25.1 teams is open but keyboard navigation seems stuck what you will learn: recover without randomly pressing keys. before you begin: teams is responsive. exactly how to do it press escape once. press tab once and listen to/observe the newly focused control. if you are in a list, try up arrow and down arrow. if you are inside a menu, use arrow keys and escape to close it. use ctrl+e/command+e to move directly to search if you need a stable starting point. use ctrl+period/command+period to confirm the current shortcut list. if the interface is still not responding, close and reopen the current pane or restart teams. what should happen: focus begins moving predictably again. if that does not happen: if the whole app is frozen rather than merely focused in an unusual region, restart teams and check for an update. practice: deliberately open a menu, close it with escape, then return to search. 25.2 other people cannot hear you what you will learn: find whether the problem is mute state, device selection, permissions, or hardware. before you begin: be in a call/meeting or open device settings. exactly how to do it check whether teams shows your microphone as muted. press ctrl+shift+m on windows or command+shift+m on mac to change the state if needed. open teams settings > devices. confirm the intended microphone is selected. speak and check any input/test feedback. check windows/macos microphone privacy permission for microsoft teams. check the headset's physical mute switch if it has one. try another known-good microphone if available. what should happen: your voice is detected and other participants can hear you. if that does not happen: if teams sees no microphone at all, solve the operating-system/hardware problem before changing meeting settings. practice: before an important meeting, verify microphone selection and mute state. 25.3 you cannot hear the meeting what you will learn: check speaker/output issues in order. before you begin: teams meeting audio should be active. exactly how to do it check the computer's master volume and mute state. open teams settings > devices. confirm the correct speaker/output device is selected. if using bluetooth headphones, confirm they are connected to the computer. check the meeting's audio connection mode. use a teams test call or operating-system sound test if available. reconnect or reselect the output device. what should happen: meeting audio comes through the intended device. if that does not happen: if other apps also have no sound, troubleshoot the operating-system audio device rather than teams alone. practice: switch between two available output devices and restore the preferred one. 25.4 you cannot find a chat or channel what you will learn: use direct navigation instead of browsing every item. before you begin: know part of the name. exactly how to do it press ctrl+g/command+g and type the chat/channel name. review matches and open the correct one. if there is no match, press ctrl+e/command+e. search for the team name, channel name, person's full name, or distinctive keyword. check whether the channel is hidden, private, shared, or outside your current organization/account. what should happen: you either find the destination or identify a membership/account reason it is unavailable. if that does not happen: if you use multiple organizations/tenants/accounts, confirm you are currently in the correct one. practice: find the same channel once with ctrl+g and once with search. 25.5 meeting join button is missing what you will learn: determine why a meeting cannot yet be joined. before you begin: open the meeting details. exactly how to do it confirm the meeting date and start time. confirm that the event is actually a teams/online meeting. look for join in the calendar item or meeting details. refresh/reopen calendar. check whether you are signed into the invited account. if you joined from a link, reopen the invitation link. if the organizer uses a lobby, remember that the join button gets you to the lobby; admission is separate. what should happen: the join option appears or you identify the reason it is unavailable. if that does not happen: if the meeting was cancelled, changed, or created without online meeting details, contact the organizer. practice: open a future meeting and identify where join will appear when available. part 26 - independent practice course level 1 - basic orientation ☐ open teams. ☐ identify search, app bar/navigation, list pane, and main content area. ☐ open the keyboard shortcuts list. ☐ close it with escape. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 2 - search and chat ☐ search for a person. ☐ open an existing chat. ☐ read recent messages. ☐ send a reply. ☐ return to the chat list. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 3 - new chat and mentions ☐ start a new chat. ☐ add a recipient. ☐ send a message. ☐ create an @mention in a draft. ☐ attach a non-sensitive practice file. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 4 - channels ☐ open a team/channel. ☐ read channel posts. ☐ reply to a channel post. ☐ return to the channels list. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 5 - calendar ☐ open calendar. ☐ find a future meeting. ☐ open its details. ☐ return to calendar. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 6 - schedule ☐ create a practice meeting. ☐ add a title and attendee. ☐ set date/time. ☐ add an agenda. ☐ send the invitation. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 7 - meeting ☐ join with mic muted. ☐ turn camera state on/off deliberately. ☐ open people. ☐ open meeting chat. ☐ turn on captions if available. ☐ leave the meeting. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 8 - sharing and devices ☐ verify microphone and speaker. ☐ start a test meeting. ☐ share a safe window. ☐ stop sharing. ☐ leave. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. level 9 - independent recovery ☐ recover from a menu with escape. ☐ use search when lost. ☐ use ctrl+g/command+g to find a destination. ☐ open teams' shortcut list to confirm a command. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you what key to press. part 27 - quick reference keyboard commands windows desktop task command show keyboard shortcuts ctrl+period (.) or alt+/ search ctrl+e open settings ctrl+comma (,) new chat ctrl+n new chat window ctrl+shift+n go to chat/channel ctrl+g close/back esc mute/unmute ctrl+shift+m camera on/off ctrl+shift+o audio call from focused contact/chat ctrl+shift+c video call from focused contact/chat ctrl+shift+u mac desktop task command show keyboard shortcuts command+period (.) search command+e open settings command+comma (,) new chat command+n go to chat/channel command+g close/back esc mute/unmute command+shift+m numbered app navigation: ctrl+number on windows and command+number on mac can open apps by their sequential position on the teams app bar. because users can reorder apps, always verify the current position before relying on a number. part 28 - official microsoft resources microsoft teams accessibility help keyboard shortcuts for microsoft teams basic tasks using a screen reader with microsoft teams use a screen reader to chat in microsoft teams use a screen reader to schedule a meeting use a screen reader to join a meeting use a screen reader to share your screen use a screen reader to make and answer calls screen reader support for microsoft teams final independence checklist ☐ i can open teams and sign in. ☐ i understand the app bar, list pane, and main content area. ☐ i can open the current keyboard-shortcuts list. ☐ i can search for people, chats, and channels. ☐ i can read and send chat messages. ☐ i can start a new chat. ☐ i can use @mentions and attach a file. ☐ i can navigate channels and read posts. ☐ i can open shared files. ☐ i can use calendar. ☐ i can schedule a meeting. ☐ i can join a meeting with deliberate mic/camera settings. ☐ i can mute/unmute, open people, use meeting chat, and leave. ☐ i can turn on captions when available. ☐ i can share and stop sharing content safely. ☐ i can check microphone, speaker, and camera settings. ☐ i can use the screen-reader procedures for my platform. ☐ i can troubleshoot common teams problems in a logical order. ☐ i know where to find microsoft's current teams accessibility documentation. most important habit: do one action, then stop and confirm what changed. in teams, this prevents accidental calls, messages, screen sharing, and navigation errors. return to all manuals

entries.title: Microsoft Word Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Microsoft Word Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: microsoft word screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual microsoft word screen reader manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide for word on windows all manuals table of contents start of manual microsoft screen reader support for word purpose: this manual is written directly to a person learning microsoft word with a screen reader. it assumes little or no prior word experience and explains what to press, what should happen, what your screen reader should announce, and how to recover when the result is different. reference version: the manual is written primarily for word for microsoft 365 on windows. many commands also work in word 2024, 2021, 2019, and 2016, but ribbon wording can differ. screen readers: core word keyboard commands are taught first. narrator, nvda, and jaws are covered separately so screen-reader commands are not mixed together. how to use this manual work through parts 1-12 before focusing on your screen reader. those sections teach word itself. do one action, stop, and listen to what changed before pressing another key. word uses both direct shortcuts and the ribbon. direct shortcuts are usually faster once memorized. alt activates ribbon keytips. after pressing alt, use the letters word announces for the tab and command you want. f6 cycles among major word regions such as document, ribbon, status bar, and panes. tab and shift+tab move between controls in dialogs and panes. arrow keys move through text, menus, lists, and ribbon controls depending on context. narrator, nvda, and jaws all work with standard windows text-editing keys. use word's built-in styles instead of making headings look like headings only with bold and larger font. save often with ctrl+s. table of contents part 1 - what microsoft word is part 2 - open word and create a document part 3 - learn the word window and ribbon part 4 - type, move, select, and edit text part 5 - save, save as, open, and close part 6 - find and replace part 7 - character and paragraph formatting part 8 - headings, styles, and navigation pane part 9 - bulleted and numbered lists part 10 - tables part 11 - links, pictures, alt text, headers, and footers part 12 - spelling, grammar, and editor part 13 - comments part 14 - track changes part 15 - accessibility checker and accessible document design part 16 - print, export to pdf, and share part 17 - narrator with word part 18 - nvda with word part 19 - jaws with word part 20 - reading long documents part 21 - braille displays with word part 22 - word online part 23 - troubleshooting part 24 - independent practice course part 25 - quick reference commands part 26 - official microsoft resources part 1 - what microsoft word is microsoft word is a word-processing application for creating, reading, editing, formatting, reviewing, and sharing documents. word documents commonly use the docx format. document body: the main area where text is typed and edited. ribbon: a set of tabs such as home, insert, layout, references, review, and view. status bar: reports information such as page number, word count, and view. navigation pane: lets you search the document and move among headings. comments pane: contains collaboration comments. review features: track changes, accept/reject, comments, compare, spelling, and accessibility tools. part 2 - open word and create a document 2.1 open word from windows search what you will learn: start microsoft word without using a mouse. before you begin: word must be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type word. use up/down arrow if more than one result appears. press enter on microsoft word. wait for word to open. what should happen: the word start screen or a document window opens. if that does not happen: if word does not appear in search, microsoft 365/word may not be installed or may use a different organization deployment. practice: open word twice using search. 2.2 create a blank document what you will learn: start a new editable document. before you begin: word is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+n. wait for a blank document. type: this is my first word practice document. press enter twice. type a second sentence. what should happen: text appears in the new document. if that does not happen: if ctrl+n opens a start screen instead of a blank file, choose blank document with tab/enter. practice: create a new document and type two short paragraphs. part 3 - learn the word window and ribbon 3.1 move between word regions with f6 what you will learn: understand where keyboard focus is. before you begin: open a document. exactly how to do it press f6 once. listen to the region or control announced. press f6 again. continue several times. use shift+f6 to move backward through the regions. stop when focus returns to the document body. what should happen: focus cycles through word's major regions. if that does not happen: if f6 seems to do nothing, make sure word is the active application and no modal dialog is open. practice: cycle through all regions once. 3.2 use ribbon keytips what you will learn: reach a ribbon command by keyboard. before you begin: be in a word document. exactly how to do it press alt. listen for ribbon keytips. press h for home. listen as focus enters the home tab. use tab/shift+tab or arrow keys through controls. press escape to leave the ribbon and return toward the document. what should happen: the home ribbon tab becomes active. if that does not happen: if pressing alt opens an application menu from another program, word may not have focus. practice: open home, insert, and review tabs using alt key sequences. part 4 - type, move, select, and edit text task command character left/right left / right arrow word left/right ctrl+left / ctrl+right line up/down up / down arrow start/end of line home / end start/end of document ctrl+home / ctrl+end select character shift+left / shift+right select word ctrl+shift+left / ctrl+shift+right select line/paragraph portions shift with navigation keys select all ctrl+a delete previous character backspace delete next character delete undo ctrl+z redo/repeat ctrl+y 4.1 correct a typing error what you will learn: move the insertion point to an exact location and replace text. before you begin: type a sentence containing one deliberate error. exactly how to do it press ctrl+left arrow to move backward one word at a time. use left/right arrow to move one character at a time. press backspace or delete to remove the incorrect character. type the correct character. use your screen reader's line or word reading command to verify the correction. what should happen: the correction occurs at the intended position. if that does not happen: if text changes in the wrong location, press ctrl+home or ctrl+end to establish a known position and navigate again. practice: create three errors and correct all three. 4.2 select and replace a word what you will learn: select text with the keyboard. before you begin: place the caret next to a word. exactly how to do it hold ctrl+shift. press left or right arrow to select the word. release the keys. type the replacement word. what should happen: the selected word is replaced. if that does not happen: if extra punctuation or spaces are selected, undo with ctrl+z and select more carefully. practice: replace three words using selection. part 5 - save, save as, open, and close task command save ctrl+s save as f12 or ctrl+shift+s depending word version/configuration open ctrl+o close document ctrl+w exit word alt+f4 5.1 save a new document what you will learn: choose a filename and location. before you begin: have an unsaved document open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+s. if the save as area appears, navigate to the desired folder/location. move to the file name field. type a descriptive filename without typing .docx unless word requires it. move to save. press enter. wait for word to return to the document. what should happen: the document is saved as a docx file. if that does not happen: if word asks about another file format, choose docx unless you intentionally need another format. practice: save a practice document to documents. 5.2 reopen a saved document what you will learn: find and open an existing word file. before you begin: know the filename or recent location. exactly how to do it press ctrl+o. use the recent list or browse. navigate to the file. press enter. wait for the document to load. use ctrl+home and begin reading. what should happen: the correct document opens. if that does not happen: if another file opens, close it with ctrl+w and verify the filename before selecting. practice: close and reopen your practice file. part 6 - find and replace 6.1 find text what you will learn: search within a document. before you begin: open a document containing several paragraphs. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. type the word or phrase you want to find. press enter if required. press tab until the results list is announced. use up/down arrow through results. press enter on a result to move to it. press escape to close the navigation pane when finished. what should happen: word moves to the selected occurrence. if that does not happen: if the navigation pane seems confusing, press escape and reopen with ctrl+f. practice: find three different words. 6.2 replace text what you will learn: replace one or all occurrences. before you begin: open a practice document. exactly how to do it press ctrl+h. type the old text in find what. press tab to replace with. type the new text. tab to find next and activate it. use replace to change only the current occurrence, or replace all only when every occurrence should change. read word's replacement count if shown. what should happen: the intended text is replaced. if that does not happen: if replace all would change unintended text, press escape and use replace one occurrence at a time. practice: replace one word safely, then undo. part 7 - character and paragraph formatting task command bold ctrl+b italic ctrl+i underline ctrl+u left align ctrl+l center ctrl+e right align ctrl+r justify ctrl+j increase font size ctrl+shift+> decrease font size ctrl+shift+< clear direct character formatting ctrl+spacebar 7.1 apply bold to existing text what you will learn: format selected text without retyping it. before you begin: have text available. exactly how to do it select the word or phrase. press ctrl+b. use your screen reader's formatting information command if available to confirm bold. press right arrow without shift to clear the selection and move the caret. what should happen: selected text becomes bold. if that does not happen: if newly typed text continues in bold unexpectedly, press ctrl+b again to toggle bold off. practice: bold and unbold a practice phrase. 7.2 change paragraph alignment what you will learn: change how a paragraph is positioned. before you begin: place the caret anywhere in a paragraph. exactly how to do it press ctrl+e to center. listen for any screen-reader formatting feedback. press ctrl+l to restore left alignment. what should happen: the paragraph alignment changes. if that does not happen: if only part of a paragraph changes unexpectedly, check whether text was selected. practice: center a heading, then restore left alignment. part 8 - headings, styles, and navigation pane built-in heading styles are critical for accessibility. they let screen readers and word's navigation pane understand document structure. task command heading 1 ctrl+alt+1 heading 2 ctrl+alt+2 heading 3 ctrl+alt+3 normal style ctrl+shift+n 8.1 apply a real heading style what you will learn: make a section navigable to screen readers. before you begin: type a short section title on its own line. exactly how to do it place the caret in the title line. press ctrl+alt+1 for heading 1, or ctrl+alt+2 for heading 2. move to the next paragraph and press ctrl+shift+n if you need to ensure normal style for body text. open navigation pane with ctrl+f. move to the headings view/tab. confirm the heading appears in the headings list. what should happen: the heading is recognized structurally, not just visually. if that does not happen: if the heading is absent from navigation pane, it may have direct visual formatting rather than a built-in heading style. practice: create heading 1 and heading 2 sections and navigate between them. heading order: use heading 1, then heading 2, then heading 3 as structure requires. do not skip levels solely to get a visual size. 8.2 navigate by headings what you will learn: jump through a long document. before you begin: the document contains built-in heading styles. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. move to the headings tab in the navigation pane. use tab/shift+tab and arrow keys until the heading list is focused. use up/down arrow through headings. press enter on the desired heading. press escape to return to the document. what should happen: the caret moves to the chosen section. if that does not happen: if only search results appear, switch the navigation pane from results to headings. practice: navigate to three headings without scrolling. part 9 - bulleted and numbered lists task command bulleted list ctrl+shift+l numbered list alt+h, n (ribbon path may continue depending gallery) increase indent tab at start of list item decrease indent shift+tab at start of list item 9.1 create a bulleted list what you will learn: create a true list that screen readers recognize. before you begin: place the caret on a blank line. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+l. type the first item. press enter. type the second item. press enter. type the third item. press enter twice to end the list. what should happen: word creates a structured bulleted list. if that does not happen: if pressing enter twice creates another blank bullet instead of ending the list, press backspace once at the empty bullet. practice: create a three-item grocery list. 9.2 create a numbered list from the ribbon what you will learn: create a structured numbered sequence. before you begin: place the caret on a blank line. exactly how to do it press alt+h. press n to open numbering. use arrow keys through numbering styles. press enter on the desired numbering style. type each item and press enter between items. press enter twice to end the list. what should happen: word numbers each item automatically. if that does not happen: if the numbering gallery does not open with the same key sequence, use alt and listen to current keytips because office updates can modify ribbon keytips. practice: create a five-step procedure. part 10 - tables simple tables are accessible when they contain a predictable grid and a clearly designated header row. avoid merged, split, or nested cells when possible. 10.1 insert a simple table what you will learn: create a table by specifying rows and columns. before you begin: place the caret where the table should appear. exactly how to do it press alt+n to open insert. use the current ribbon keytip for table, often t. choose insert table if needed. enter the number of columns. enter the number of rows. activate ok/insert. type the first cell. press tab to move to the next cell. continue through the table. what should happen: a table appears and tab moves from cell to cell. if that does not happen: if you reach the last cell and press tab, word may add another row. use shift+tab to move back if that was accidental. practice: create a 3-column by 4-row table. 10.2 make the first row a header row what you will learn: help screen readers identify column names. before you begin: the table has a first row containing column headings. exactly how to do it place the caret anywhere in the table. use the table design/layout contextual tabs that appear on the ribbon. locate the header row option under table style options. turn header row on. use accessibility checker afterward to verify the table. what should happen: word treats the first row as a header row in supported accessibility contexts. if that does not happen: if the contextual table tabs do not appear, make sure the caret is inside the table. practice: create a name, date, status table with a header row. avoid: merged cells, split cells, nested tables, and completely blank structural rows/columns can make screen-reader navigation difficult. part 11 - links, pictures, alt text, headers, and footers 11.1 insert a hyperlink with meaningful text what you will learn: create a link that makes sense when read out of context. before you begin: select descriptive text such as 'microsoft accessibility support'. exactly how to do it press ctrl+k. move to the address field. type or paste the web address. press enter. read the linked text to confirm it is descriptive. what should happen: the selected text becomes a hyperlink. if that does not happen: if the visible text is a raw url, consider replacing it with descriptive text unless the url itself is necessary. practice: create one descriptive hyperlink. 11.2 add alt text to an image what you will learn: make an image understandable to someone who cannot see it. before you begin: insert or select a picture. exactly how to do it select the image using word's object navigation or tab/shift+tab. open the image context menu with shift+f10 or use picture format. open alt text. type a concise description that communicates the image's purpose/content. if the image is purely decorative, mark it decorative instead of writing meaningless alt text. close the alt text pane. what should happen: the image has meaningful alternative text or is marked decorative. if that does not happen: if alt text is not available from the context menu, use the picture format/accessibility controls or accessibility assistant. practice: add alt text to a practice image. 11.3 add a page number in the footer what you will learn: insert repeated page numbers. before you begin: open a document with more than one page. exactly how to do it press alt+n for insert. use the current ribbon keytip for page number. choose bottom of page or another location. choose a simple page-number style. press escape when finished editing the header/footer. what should happen: page numbers appear on pages. if that does not happen: if the header/footer remains active, press escape or use the close header and footer command. practice: insert page numbers, then remove them in a copy. accessibility caution: do not place essential document content only in headers or footers. screen-reader users may not encounter header/footer information in the normal reading flow. part 12 - spelling, grammar, and editor 12.1 review spelling and grammar what you will learn: use word's editor to correct errors one by one. before you begin: have a document with a deliberate spelling error. exactly how to do it press f7. wait for editor/proofing to open. listen to the flagged word and suggestion. use tab and arrow keys through suggestions/actions. choose the correct suggestion with enter. use ignore only when the original word is intentionally correct. continue until word reports the review is complete or close editor. what should happen: the error is corrected or intentionally ignored. if that does not happen: if f7 performs another laptop function, use fn+f7 or review > editor. practice: create three spelling errors and correct them. part 13 - comments 13.1 add a comment what you will learn: attach a collaboration note to selected text. before you begin: open a document and select a word or phrase. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+m. wait for the comment box/pane. type the comment. post the comment using the post comment button or current keyboard command. return to the document. what should happen: a comment is attached to the selected text. if that does not happen: if the comment is not posted, verify that you activated post rather than simply moving focus away. practice: add a comment to a practice sentence. 13.2 read and navigate comments what you will learn: review collaboration feedback. before you begin: open a document containing comments. exactly how to do it open the review tab with alt+r. navigate to comments or the comments pane. use tab and arrow keys through comments. listen for author and comment text. use resolve/delete only when you intend to change review history. what should happen: you can read comments independently. if that does not happen: if focus jumps back into the document, reopen the comments pane and use f6/shift+f6 to move among word regions. practice: read two comments and return to the document. part 14 - track changes task command toggle track changes ctrl+shift+e review tab alt+r 14.1 turn track changes on and off what you will learn: record edits for review. before you begin: open a practice document. exactly how to do it press ctrl+shift+e. listen for the track changes state if your screen reader announces it. type a short word or delete one character. press ctrl+shift+e again to stop tracking new changes. what should happen: word marks the edit as a tracked change while tracking is on. if that does not happen: if the state is unclear, open review with alt+r and inspect track changes. practice: track one insertion and one deletion. 14.2 accept or reject changes what you will learn: resolve revisions one at a time. before you begin: open a document containing tracked changes and use all markup for best review. exactly how to do it press alt+r. navigate to next change. read the changed content and change type. choose accept or reject. move to the next change. repeat until all intended changes are reviewed. what should happen: accepted changes become permanent; rejected changes are removed/reverted. if that does not happen: if word appears to hide changes, confirm the display option is all markup rather than no markup. practice: accept one practice change and reject another. direct track changes shortcut: microsoft currently documents ctrl+shift+e to toggle track changes in word for windows. part 15 - accessibility checker and accessible document design use built-in title, subtitle, and heading styles. use headings in logical order. use meaningful link text. add alt text to informative images and mark decorative images decorative. use simple tables with header rows. do not use color alone to convey meaning. use sufficient color contrast. avoid long runs of all caps and overly decorative fonts. give documents a meaningful title. run accessibility checker/accessibility assistant before sharing. 15.1 run accessibility checker what you will learn: find common accessibility problems. before you begin: open a finished practice document. exactly how to do it open review with alt+r. navigate to check accessibility/accessibility. open accessibility checker or accessibility assistant. move through issues in the accessibility pane. select an issue. read why it is a problem and the recommended fix. correct the issue in the document. repeat until no important issues remain. what should happen: the document has fewer accessibility barriers. if that does not happen: if the accessibility command is unavailable, verify you are using a supported word version and not a restricted document. practice: run it on your practice document and fix at least two issues. accessibility assistant: current word for microsoft 365 on windows includes accessibility assistant, which can surface accessibility issues while you work. part 16 - print, export to pdf, and share 16.1 print with keyboard what you will learn: review the selected printer and print settings before printing. before you begin: have a document open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+p. listen to the selected printer. use tab through copies, page range, orientation, paper size, and other settings. confirm the printer and number of copies. move to print. press enter. what should happen: the document is sent to the selected printer. if that does not happen: if the wrong printer is selected, change it before activating print. practice: open print, review settings, then cancel. 16.2 export/save as pdf what you will learn: create a pdf copy while keeping the word original. before you begin: save the docx first. exactly how to do it open file with alt+f. navigate to save as or export. choose pdf as the file type. enter a filename/location. if an accessibility/tagging option is available, keep document structure tags enabled. save. return to word and confirm the original docx remains open. what should happen: a pdf copy is created. if that does not happen: if the pdf is intended for accessibility, verify it after export because not every word feature converts perfectly. practice: export a practice document and compare filenames. 16.3 share a document what you will learn: share through microsoft 365 when available. before you begin: the document is saved to onedrive/sharepoint if cloud sharing is required. exactly how to do it open share using the share button or file > share. enter the recipient's email address. review permissions such as can edit or can view. add a message if needed. confirm the recipient and permission. activate send/share. what should happen: the recipient receives access according to the selected permission. if that does not happen: if share is unavailable, the file may be stored only locally or your account may not have cloud sharing enabled. practice: open share and inspect permission choices without sending. part 17 - narrator with word narrator works with word using standard windows keyboard focus plus narrator reading commands. word's own shortcuts still perform document actions. task command start/stop narrator windows+ctrl+enter narrator key caps lock or insert input learning narrator+1 next/previous item narrator+right/left arrow primary action narrator+enter narrator settings windows+ctrl+n 17.1 read and edit a word document with narrator what you will learn: use narrator without confusing word commands and narrator commands. before you begin: narrator is on and a word document is open. exactly how to do it press ctrl+home to move to the start of the document. use down arrow to move line by line. use ctrl+right arrow to move by word. use narrator reading commands when you need more detailed review. type text normally in the document body. use word shortcuts such as ctrl+b or ctrl+s normally. use narrator+1 input learning when you forget a narrator command. what should happen: narrator reads word while word editing shortcuts continue to work. if that does not happen: if narrator item navigation moves out of the document unexpectedly, use f6/shift+f6 or click-free tab navigation to return to the document area. practice: read and edit two paragraphs. 17.2 navigate headings with narrator and word navigation pane what you will learn: jump by document structure. before you begin: the document contains built-in heading styles. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. move to the headings list. use arrow keys through headings. press enter on the desired heading. press escape. use narrator to read from the new location. what should happen: the document moves to the selected heading. if that does not happen: if the heading list is empty, the document may not use real heading styles. practice: navigate to three headings. part 18 - nvda with word nvda follows word's editing caret and keyboard focus. standard word navigation keys are usually the fastest way to edit; nvda adds speech, formatting, object, and review commands. task command nvda menu nvda+n input help nvda+1 say title nvda+t say focused object nvda+tab report formatting nvda+f say current line nvda+up arrow in desktop layout 18.1 review formatting with nvda what you will learn: hear font and style information for text. before you begin: open a formatted word document with nvda. exactly how to do it move the caret into the text you want to inspect. press nvda+f. listen for font, size, style, color, alignment, and other available formatting information. move to another paragraph and repeat. use word's built-in style commands to correct formatting if needed. what should happen: nvda reports formatting at the caret. if that does not happen: if the command differs in your nvda keyboard layout, use nvda+1 input help or the nvda command reference. practice: compare normal text and a heading 1 paragraph. 18.2 use word headings with nvda what you will learn: navigate structure using word rather than web browse mode. before you begin: open a structured docx. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f to open navigation pane. move to headings. use arrows through headings. press enter on a heading. press escape. continue reading/editing. what should happen: focus moves to the selected heading. if that does not happen: if nvda browse mode behavior appears unexpectedly, remember that desktop word is not a normal webpage; rely on word's navigation pane and document commands. practice: navigate a structured document. part 19 - jaws with word jaws provides extensive word support while standard word shortcuts remain active. task command keyboard help insert+1 hot key help insert+h windows key help insert+w jaws command search insert+space, then j say title insert+t say line insert+up arrow say word insert+numpad5 say font insert+f 19.1 review text and formatting with jaws what you will learn: use jaws reading commands while editing word. before you begin: open a word document with jaws. exactly how to do it press ctrl+home. use down arrow or jaws say line to read. use ctrl+right arrow through words. press insert+f to hear font/format information. use standard word shortcuts to change text/formatting. press insert+h when you need word-specific jaws hotkeys. what should happen: jaws reads word and reports formatting. if that does not happen: if a jaws command is forgotten, use insert+1 or command search instead of guessing. practice: compare formatting in a heading and body paragraph. 19.2 use jaws with navigation pane what you will learn: move by real headings. before you begin: the document uses heading styles. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. move to headings in navigation pane. use up/down arrow through headings. press enter. press escape. use jaws reading commands at the new location. what should happen: the caret moves to the chosen section. if that does not happen: if the heading list is empty, correct the document's style structure. practice: navigate to three headings. part 20 - reading long documents use ctrl+home and ctrl+end to establish a known position. use ctrl+f for search and navigation pane. use built-in headings to jump between sections. use page up/page down for larger visual/page movement, but rely on headings/search for precise navigation. use comments and track changes panes separately from the document body. save before large edits. for very long documents, create a structured heading hierarchy before doing detailed editing. 20.1 build a navigation strategy what you will learn: read a long document without getting lost. before you begin: open a document with several headings. exactly how to do it press ctrl+home. open navigation pane with ctrl+f. review the heading list. move to a middle section. search for a keyword within that section/document. press escape and read from the result. use ctrl+home to return to the start when finished. what should happen: you can move intentionally rather than line-by-line through the entire file. if that does not happen: if the document has no headings, search and page navigation are still available, but consider adding proper styles if you own the document. practice: navigate a document by heading, search result, and beginning/end. part 21 - braille displays with word a braille display works through the active screen reader. word itself does not directly control the braille display. narrator braille settings are configured in windows narrator settings. nvda braille displays are configured in nvda settings > braille. jaws braille displays are configured in jaws braille/display settings. routing keys should move the editing caret to the braille cell's represented position when supported. braille panning moves through text beyond the display's cell width. translation tables and contracted/uncontracted braille are screen-reader settings, not word document formatting. 21.1 test word with a braille display what you will learn: verify output, input, and routing. before you begin: connect the display and configure it in your screen reader. exactly how to do it open word and type a short sentence. read the sentence on the braille display. pan right/left if the sentence exceeds the display width. press a routing key over a word. type one character and confirm it appears at the intended location. undo the test change with ctrl+z. what should happen: braille follows the word caret and routing works. if that does not happen: if braille changes in other apps but not word, restart word/screen reader and verify focus is in the document body. practice: perform output, input, routing. part 22 - word online word for the web runs inside a browser, so browser and screen-reader web modes can interact with word's own shortcuts. word for the web may use alt+windows logo key combinations for ribbon commands. screen reader browse/scan/virtual modes may need to be adjusted when editing. some desktop features are simplified or unavailable online. use the desktop word manual sections as concepts, but verify web-specific shortcuts in microsoft's current word for the web documentation. part 23 - troubleshooting 23.1 typing replaces text unexpectedly what you will learn: check whether text is selected or overwrite behavior is active. before you begin: you are editing a document. exactly how to do it press escape to clear temporary menus. press an arrow key without shift to clear any selection. type one test character. if text still overwrites existing characters, check word's advanced editing settings for overtype behavior. undo test changes with ctrl+z. what should happen: typing inserts text normally. if that does not happen: if replacement occurs only after selecting text, that is normal word behavior: typing replaces the selection. practice: practice selecting a word and observe deliberate replacement. 23.2 the ribbon has focus and you cannot type what you will learn: return to the document body. before you begin: word is open. exactly how to do it press escape once or twice. press f6 until the document area is announced. press an arrow key. type a test character. undo with ctrl+z. what should happen: the caret is back in the document. if that does not happen: if f6 cycles among panes without reaching the document, close modal panes/dialogs first. practice: move to ribbon with alt, then recover to document. 23.3 screen reader reads very little or nothing what you will learn: separate a word-focus problem from an audio/screen-reader problem. before you begin: word is open. exactly how to do it press alt+tab away from word and confirm the screen reader speaks another app. if it does, alt+tab back to word. press f6 until document is focused. press ctrl+home and down arrow. if speech is still absent, use your screen reader's 'say line/current item' command. restart the screen reader only after checking focus. what should happen: speech resumes in word. if that does not happen: if the screen reader is silent everywhere, troubleshoot system audio/screen reader instead of word. practice: memorize: test another app > return > f6 > ctrl+home > read command. 23.4 navigation pane shows no headings what you will learn: determine whether the document has real heading styles. before you begin: open navigation pane. exactly how to do it move to headings. if the list is empty, return to a visible section title. place the caret in the title. apply heading 1 or heading 2 with ctrl+alt+1/2. return to navigation pane. what should happen: the newly styled heading appears. if that does not happen: if not, save/reopen the document and verify that the paragraph uses a built-in heading style. practice: convert two visually formatted titles into real headings. part 24 - independent practice course level 1 - create and save ☐ open word. ☐ create blank document. ☐ type two paragraphs. ☐ save as docx. ☐ close and reopen. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 2 - editing ☐ move by character and word. ☐ select a word. ☐ replace it. ☐ undo/redo. ☐ find text. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 3 - formatting ☐ bold text. ☐ change alignment. ☐ create heading 1 and heading 2. ☐ open navigation pane. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 4 - lists and tables ☐ create a bulleted list. ☐ create a numbered list. ☐ insert a 3x4 table. ☐ create a header row. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 5 - review ☐ run spelling/grammar. ☐ add a comment. ☐ turn on track changes. ☐ accept one change. ☐ reject one change. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 6 - accessibility ☐ add descriptive hyperlink. ☐ add image alt text. ☐ run accessibility checker. ☐ fix two issues. ☐ verify heading order. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 7 - screen reader ☐ use narrator, nvda, or jaws help. ☐ read formatting. ☐ navigate headings. ☐ recover from ribbon focus. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 8 - braille ☐ read word text on braille if used. ☐ pan text. ☐ use routing key. ☐ correct one character. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 9 - independent document ☐ create a one-page document with title, headings, list, table, link, and accessible structure. ☐ run accessibility checker. ☐ save docx and pdf. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. part 25 - quick reference commands word editing task command new document ctrl+n open ctrl+o save ctrl+s print ctrl+p close document ctrl+w undo / redo ctrl+z / ctrl+y find / replace ctrl+f / ctrl+h select all ctrl+a copy / cut / paste ctrl+c / ctrl+x / ctrl+v bold / italic / underline ctrl+b / ctrl+i / ctrl+u heading 1 / 2 / 3 ctrl+alt+1 / 2 / 3 normal style ctrl+shift+n bulleted list ctrl+shift+l insert hyperlink ctrl+k new comment ctrl+alt+m track changes ctrl+shift+e spelling/grammar f7 switch word regions f6 / shift+f6 narrator task command start/stop windows+ctrl+enter input learning narrator+1 next/previous item narrator+right/left arrow primary action narrator+enter settings windows+ctrl+n nvda task command menu nvda+n input help nvda+1 say title nvda+t say focused object nvda+tab report formatting nvda+f jaws task command keyboard help insert+1 hot key help insert+h command search insert+space, then j say title insert+t say line insert+up arrow say font insert+f part 26 - official microsoft resources screen reader support for word basic tasks using a screen reader with word keyboard shortcuts in word track and review changes with a screen reader make word documents accessible accessibility assistant in word create headers or footers with a screen reader final independence checklist ☐ i can open word and create a document. ☐ i can type, move, select, edit, undo, and redo. ☐ i can save, reopen, and close documents. ☐ i can use find and replace. ☐ i can apply character and paragraph formatting. ☐ i can create real headings and navigate them. ☐ i can create accessible lists and simple tables. ☐ i can insert descriptive links and alt text. ☐ i can run spelling and grammar review. ☐ i can add and read comments. ☐ i can use track changes and accept/reject revisions. ☐ i can run accessibility checker/accessibility assistant. ☐ i can print, export to pdf, and share. ☐ i can use word with narrator, nvda, or jaws. ☐ i understand that braille is configured through the screen reader. ☐ i can troubleshoot focus, speech, typing, and heading problems. most important habit: in word, separate three things in your mind: the document caret, word's ribbon/panes, and your screen reader. if a command behaves unexpectedly, first determine which of those currently has focus. return to all manuals

entries.title: NLS Braille eReader Accessible Manual
entries.snippet: Detailed NLS Braille eReader manual covering both HumanWare and Zoomax models.
entries.text: nls braille ereader manual - accessible learning center accessible technology manual nls braille ereader accessible manual a step-by-step guide for both humanware and zoomax nls braille ereaders. all manuals ten nls braille ereader lessons my progress purpose and setup this manual supports independent practice with nls braille ereader on windows. use the exact software version, device model, account permissions, and workplace policy available to you. commands and labels can change after updates. start jaws before opening the application or connecting a braille device. use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focus, and insert+1 for keyboard help. practice with fictional, public, instructor-provided, or redacted information only. never submit passwords, recovery codes, government identifiers, protected books, or private workplace data. save a backup before changing, deleting, converting, or remediating a file. identify your model before using commands zoomax: has six display keys labeled d1 through d6, four system keys labeled s1 through s4, and five navigation keys. s1 opens the main menu. humanware: uses four thumb keys for menu movement
