want. press shift+tab or alt+left arrow to return when needed. what should happen: settings > accessibility opens. if that does not happen: if another app receives u instead, make sure the windows key is held down. practice: open accessibility, enter magnifier, return, then enter keyboard. search alternative: press windows, type the name of a feature such as 'live captions' or 'magnifier settings,' then press enter on the matching settings result. part 3 - text size and visual effects 3.1 increase text size without enlarging everything what you will learn: make text easier to read while keeping overall screen layout similar. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open text size. move to the text size slider. increase the percentage gradually. use the preview area to judge the result. activate apply. wait for windows to update text. what should happen: text becomes larger across supported windows interfaces without applying full-screen magnification. if that does not happen: if controls become crowded, reduce the percentage and reapply. practice: try one moderate increase and restore it if not useful. 3.2 reduce animation and transparency what you will learn: reduce motion and visual distraction. before you begin: open accessibility > visual effects. exactly how to do it find animation effects. turn it off if movement is distracting. find transparency effects. turn it off if translucent backgrounds reduce readability. review notification-dismiss timing on the same page when available. what should happen: windows uses fewer animations and/or more solid backgrounds. if that does not happen: some apps have their own animation settings and may not follow every windows preference. practice: toggle each setting and compare. part 4 - mouse pointer and touch 4.1 make the mouse pointer easier to see what you will learn: increase pointer size or use a more visible pointer style. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open mouse pointer and touch. move to the pointer-size slider. increase size gradually. move to mouse pointer style. choose white, black, inverted, or another visible style. if offered, choose a custom pointer color. what should happen: the pointer becomes easier to locate. if that does not happen: if the pointer is too large and covers controls, reduce its size. practice: try two sizes and two pointer styles. touch indicator: on touch-capable devices, windows can show a visual touch indicator so finger contact is easier to see. part 5 - text cursor 5.1 make the text cursor easier to find what you will learn: add a visible indicator around the insertion caret. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open text cursor. turn text cursor indicator on. adjust the indicator size. choose a high-visibility color. adjust text cursor thickness if needed. open notepad and type a sentence to test the caret. what should happen: the insertion point is easier to locate in supported text fields. if that does not happen: if the indicator is distracting, reduce size or turn it off while retaining a thicker cursor. practice: test in notepad and a browser edit field. part 6 - magnifier task command / path turn magnifier on windows+plus turn magnifier off windows+escape zoom in / out windows+plus / windows+minus open magnifier settings windows+ctrl+m pan ctrl+alt+arrow keys invert colors ctrl+alt+i 6.1 start and control magnifier what you will learn: enlarge screen content quickly. before you begin: windows is running. exactly how to do it press windows+plus. press windows+plus again to increase magnification. press windows+minus to reduce magnification. use ctrl+alt+arrow keys to pan if your current magnifier view supports it. press windows+escape to turn magnifier off. what should happen: the screen enlarges and then returns to normal. if that does not happen: if the keyboard has a layout where plus requires shift, hold windows and press the key that produces plus. practice: turn magnifier on, change zoom twice, then turn it off. 6.2 choose a magnifier view what you will learn: select the magnification style that fits the task. before you begin: magnifier is on. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+m. move to view. choose full screen, lens, or docked when available. return to the application and test navigation. open settings again to choose another view. what should happen: magnification behaves according to the selected view. if that does not happen: multi-monitor and app behavior can differ; choose the view that keeps orientation easiest. practice: test all available views. part 7 - magnifier reading 7.1 have magnifier read text aloud what you will learn: combine visual magnification with spoken reading. before you begin: magnifier is on. exactly how to do it press ctrl+alt+enter using the default magnifier reading modifier. listen as magnifier begins reading. press any key to stop. press ctrl+alt+k for the next sentence. press ctrl+alt+h for the previous sentence. what should happen: magnifier reads text aloud while magnifying it. if that does not happen: the reading modifier can be changed in magnifier settings. if you also use narrator, avoid assigning conflicting modifier keys. practice: read a short paragraph and move by sentence. mouse reading: with the default modifier, ctrl+alt plus a left mouse click can start reading from the clicked location. part 8 - color filters 8.1 turn on a color filter what you will learn: adjust color presentation for color-vision or sensitivity needs. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open color filters. turn color filters on. choose a filter that improves distinction or comfort. open a familiar image or webpage and compare. return to color filters to choose another filter or turn the feature off. what should happen: windows changes displayed colors without changing the underlying files. if that does not happen: if screenshots are used for color-critical work, remember the filter changes what you see, not the source content. practice: compare two filters. shortcut: when enabled in settings, windows+ctrl+c can toggle color filters. part 9 - contrast themes 9.1 apply a contrast theme what you will learn: increase separation between foreground and background elements. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open contrast themes. open the theme list. choose a theme such as aquatic, desert, dusk, or night sky when available. activate apply. wait for windows to redraw. open several apps to test readability. what should happen: windows uses a high-contrast color scheme across supported apps. if that does not happen: some websites/apps may need their own contrast settings. if text becomes harder to distinguish, choose another theme or none. practice: apply one theme and then return to your original setting. keyboard shortcut: left alt+left shift+print screen toggles contrast/high-contrast behavior on supported systems when the shortcut is enabled. part 10 - narrator overview narrator is windows 11's built-in screen reader. this manual gives an overview; a separate narrator-focused manual can teach the complete command set. task command / path start/stop narrator windows+ctrl+enter narrator settings windows+ctrl+n input learning narrator+1 toggle scan mode narrator+space 10.1 start narrator from windows what you will learn: use built-in speech access without installing another screen reader. before you begin: windows is running. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+enter. wait for narrator to speak. press narrator+1 to enter input learning. press a few harmless keys to hear their functions. press narrator+1 again to leave input learning. press windows+ctrl+enter to stop narrator. what should happen: narrator starts and stops without changing your files. if that does not happen: if the shortcut is disabled by policy or hardware, open windows+u > narrator and turn it on there. practice: start, practice, and stop narrator. part 11 - live captions 11.1 turn on live captions what you will learn: create on-screen captions for audio playing through the pc. before you begin: open windows 11 with an internet connection available for initial language setup if required. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+l. wait for the live captions window/bar. if prompted, choose/download the caption language package. play a video or other speech audio. read the captions. open caption settings to choose position/style if desired. close live captions when finished. what should happen: windows displays automated captions for supported audio. if that does not happen: captions may be inaccurate and depend on language/support. do not treat automated captions as a certified transcript. practice: caption a short known video and compare accuracy. privacy: current windows live captions processing is designed to run on-device for supported scenarios after required language components are installed, but feature behavior can vary by device/version. part 12 - audio, mono audio, and visual alerts 12.1 turn on mono audio what you will learn: send left and right audio channels into one combined channel. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it open audio. find mono audio. turn it on. play stereo audio and listen through one ear/headphone channel if appropriate. turn mono audio off if stereo separation is preferred. what should happen: both channels are combined so information from either side is not lost when listening with one channel. if that does not happen: if the sound seems less spatial, that is expected; mono removes stereo separation. practice: compare stereo and mono. 12.2 flash the screen for audio notifications what you will learn: add a visual alert when windows plays notification sounds. before you begin: open accessibility > audio. exactly how to do it find flash my screen during audio notifications. open the choice list. choose title bar, active window, entire screen, or another offered option. trigger a safe windows notification to test. what should happen: a visual flash accompanies supported audio notifications. if that does not happen: if the flash is uncomfortable, choose a smaller visual area or turn it off. practice: test one flash option. 12.3 make notifications stay visible longer what you will learn: increase reading time for temporary notifications. before you begin: open accessibility > visual effects. exactly how to do it find dismiss notifications after this amount of time. open the list. choose a longer duration. trigger a safe notification and observe how long it remains. what should happen: notifications stay on screen longer. if that does not happen: very long durations can increase clutter; choose the minimum that works. practice: compare two durations. part 13 - hearing devices windows 11 can support compatible hearing devices and bluetooth audio devices. available controls depend on the pc's bluetooth hardware, windows version, and the hearing device. 13.1 look for hearing device settings what you will learn: determine whether windows exposes dedicated hearing-device controls. before you begin: open windows+u. exactly how to do it look for hearing devices under the hearing section. open it if present. review detected/supported device options. if the page is absent, open settings > bluetooth & devices and check normal bluetooth audio pairing. follow the hearing-device manufacturer's current pairing procedure. what should happen: compatible hardware can be paired/configured where supported. if that does not happen: not every pc or hearing device supports every windows hearing-device feature. practice: locate the settings without changing a working configuration. part 14 - voice access voice access lets you control windows and dictate text by voice. microsoft documents that it works without an internet connection after the required speech language is installed. 14.1 start voice access what you will learn: control windows using spoken commands. before you begin: use a working microphone. exactly how to do it press windows+u. open speech. turn voice access on, or search start for voice access. if this is the first run, complete the language/speech-model setup. follow the voice access guide/tutorial. say 'voice access wake up' when the microphone is in the listening state if supported. use basic commands such as 'open start,' 'open settings,' or 'click <control name>'. what should happen: windows responds to supported spoken commands. if that does not happen: if recognition is poor, check microphone selection, ambient noise, and selected voice-access language. practice: open and close one app entirely by voice. 14.2 use numbers/grid when a control has no easy name what you will learn: select controls visually by voice. before you begin: voice access is listening. exactly how to do it say 'show numbers' to label clickable items when supported. say the number shown on the intended control. if a target cannot be selected reliably, say 'show grid'. narrow the grid by speaking the numbered region until the target is reached. say 'click' or the displayed number as instructed. what should happen: voice access activates otherwise hard-to-name controls. if that does not happen: exact wording can vary with current voice access command grammar; use the built-in command guide. practice: use number overlays on a safe settings page. voice shortcuts: current voice access supports custom voice shortcuts for frequently repeated tasks in supported configurations. part 15 - voice typing 15.1 dictate text with voice typing what you will learn: enter text by speech without controlling the whole computer. before you begin: place the caret in an edit field. exactly how to do it press windows+h. wait for the voice typing panel to indicate listening. speak a short sentence. say punctuation explicitly if automatic punctuation is not enabled. press windows+h again or activate the microphone control to stop. what should happen: speech is converted to text in the active field. if that does not happen: voice typing normally needs an appropriate speech service/network configuration, unlike voice access's offline control capability. practice: dictate two sentences and correct errors by keyboard. difference: voice access controls the pc and can also author text. voice typing is primarily for dictation into the active text field. part 16 - on-screen keyboard task command / path turn on-screen keyboard on/off windows+ctrl+o settings path windows+u > keyboard > on-screen keyboard 16.1 use the on-screen keyboard what you will learn: type without relying on a full physical keyboard. before you begin: open a safe text field. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+o. wait for the osk to appear. use a mouse, pointing device, touch, or scanning/switch method to choose letters. type a short word. press windows+ctrl+o again to close the osk. what should happen: a visual keyboard allows input through alternate pointing/switch methods. if that does not happen: the touch keyboard is a separate feature from the accessibility on-screen keyboard. practice: type your name or a practice phrase. part 17 - sticky keys, filter keys, and toggle keys 17.1 turn on sticky keys what you will learn: press multi-key shortcuts one key at a time. before you begin: open windows+u > keyboard. exactly how to do it turn sticky keys on. open its options. decide whether to allow the shift-key shortcut and sounds/indicator. test ctrl+s by pressing ctrl, releasing it, then pressing s. turn sticky keys off if you do not need it. what should happen: windows holds modifier keys logically so simultaneous keypresses are not required. if that does not happen: if sticky keys turns on unexpectedly after pressing shift five times, change its shortcut option. practice: use one three-key shortcut one key at a time. 17.2 use filter keys what you will learn: ignore brief or repeated accidental keypresses. before you begin: open accessibility > keyboard. exactly how to do it turn filter keys on. open its detailed settings. review options such as slow keys, bounce keys, and repeat keys. change only one timing value at a time. test typing in notepad. adjust or turn the feature off if typing becomes too slow. what should happen: windows filters keystrokes according to the selected sensitivity/timing. if that does not happen: aggressive settings can make the keyboard seem unresponsive; return to windows+u and reduce delays. practice: test with a disposable text document. 17.3 use toggle keys what you will learn: hear feedback when lock keys change state. before you begin: open accessibility > keyboard. exactly how to do it turn toggle keys on. press caps lock. listen for the state-change sound. press num lock if the keyboard has it. return to the desired lock state. what should happen: windows provides an audio cue for supported lock keys. if that does not happen: if audio is muted or unavailable, use another status method. practice: toggle caps lock twice. part 18 - mouse keys 18.1 control the pointer with the numeric keypad what you will learn: move/click the mouse pointer without moving a physical mouse. before you begin: a keyboard with numeric keypad is available. exactly how to do it press windows+u. open mouse. turn mouse keys on. review speed and acceleration settings. use the numeric keypad to move the pointer according to the windows mouse keys layout. use the mouse keys click/select controls to activate a safe desktop item. turn mouse keys off if not needed. what should happen: the numeric keypad controls the pointer. if that does not happen: laptop keyboards without a separate numeric keypad may not provide a convenient mouse keys layout. practice: move the pointer to four screen quadrants and return. part 19 - touch and pen accessibility touch-capable windows devices can expose touch indicators, touch keyboard controls, and pen settings. availability depends on hardware. use mouse pointer and touch settings to make touch contact easier to see. use settings > bluetooth & devices > pen & windows ink for pen behavior on supported devices. touch gestures can replace some mouse actions, but accessibility features such as narrator also have their own touch gesture sets. do not confuse the windows touch keyboard with the accessibility on-screen keyboard. part 20 - eye control eye control lets compatible eye-tracking hardware control windows and type without a conventional mouse/keyboard. 20.1 find eye control settings what you will learn: determine whether your system supports eye control. before you begin: a compatible eye tracker must be installed/configured. exactly how to do it press windows+u. open eye control. if the control is available, turn it on. follow the hardware calibration/setup steps. use the eye-control launchpad to practice pointer selection and typing. what should happen: windows exposes eye-controlled pointer/keyboard features when supported hardware is detected. if that does not happen: if eye control is unavailable, verify that the tracker model and drivers support current windows 11 eye control. practice: locate the page and read the setup requirements. part 21 - focus, notifications, and visual clutter 21.1 reduce visual distraction what you will learn: simplify the windows desktop/taskbar and reduce motion. before you begin: open settings. exactly how to do it open accessibility > visual effects and turn off animation effects if helpful. increase notification duration only if needed. open personalization > taskbar. hide taskbar items you do not use, such as widgets or task view if appropriate. review taskbar flashing/badges and automatic hiding. keep only settings that improve focus. what should happen: the desktop presents fewer competing visual cues. if that does not happen: hiding a feature does not uninstall it; restore items later if needed. practice: reduce one source of clutter and assess the effect. 21.2 use do not disturb / focus what you will learn: reduce interruptions during concentrated work. before you begin: open settings > system > notifications or search for do not disturb/focus. exactly how to do it turn on do not disturb for a short test period. review which priority notifications can still appear. open focus if available and start a short focus session. end the session and restore normal notifications. what should happen: nonpriority interruptions are reduced during the chosen period. if that does not happen: do not suppress safety-critical/work-required notifications without understanding the consequences. practice: run one short test session. part 22 - accessibility flyout and sign-in screen 22.1 open quick accessibility controls what you will learn: reach common accessibility features quickly. before you begin: windows is running. exactly how to do it press windows+a to open quick settings. move to accessibility. press enter. review the available quick toggles such as narrator, magnifier, live captions, sticky keys, or color filters depending on configuration. press escape to close. what should happen: common accessibility features can be toggled without opening the full settings app. if that does not happen: the exact flyout choices can vary by windows version and configuration. practice: open and close the accessibility flyout. sign-in screen: windows also provides an accessibility button on the sign-in screen so supported features can be enabled before signing in. part 23 - windows hello and easier sign-in windows hello can reduce reliance on repeatedly typing a password by using a pin, fingerprint, or face recognition when supported. 23.1 review sign-in options what you will learn: choose an accessible authentication method without weakening account security. before you begin: open settings. exactly how to do it open accounts > sign-in options. review windows hello face, fingerprint, pin, security key, and other available methods. choose only hardware-supported options you can use reliably. keep account recovery information current. what should happen: you understand the available sign-in methods. if that does not happen: do not remove the only sign-in/recovery method until a replacement has been tested. practice: inspect available options without changing them. part 24 - combining features safely magnifier + narrator: useful when both enlarged visuals and speech are needed. magnifier + contrast theme: can increase visual clarity but may be too intense for some users. sticky keys + keyboard shortcuts: lets modifier combinations be entered sequentially. live captions + mono audio: combines text access with simplified audio routing. voice access + on-screen keyboard: offers alternative interaction methods if speech or pointing becomes temporarily difficult. color filters + contrast themes can interact strongly; test them separately before combining. do not assign the same modifier shortcut to two assistive technologies if it causes conflicts. 24.1 build a personal accessibility profile what you will learn: create a repeatable set of settings that work together. before you begin: choose two or three features relevant to your access needs. exactly how to do it write down the starting settings. enable the first feature and test for five minutes. enable the second and test again. note any shortcut or visual conflicts. keep the combination only if it improves access. record how to turn each feature off. what should happen: you have a controlled, reversible combination rather than a collection of accidental settings. if that does not happen: if the computer becomes difficult to use, disable the most recently changed feature first. practice: create one two-feature profile. part 25 - privacy and security voice features use microphone access; verify which apps/services have microphone permission. live captions and speech recognition can expose sensitive spoken content on screen. screen-reader speech may be overheard in public settings. windows hello biometric data and sign-in methods should be protected like other authentication credentials. do not enable remote-assistance or third-party accessibility software merely because a pop-up claims it is required. accessibility settings are not a substitute for account security, device encryption, backups, and software updates. on shared computers, restore accessibility settings only if doing so will not remove another person's needed access. part 26 - troubleshooting 26.1 the screen suddenly looks very large what you will learn: check magnifier before changing display resolution. before you begin: everything is enlarged. exactly how to do it press windows+escape. if magnifier closes, stop troubleshooting. if not, press windows+u and open magnifier. verify magnifier is off. only then inspect display scaling/resolution. what should happen: accidental magnifier activation is ruled out quickly. if that does not happen: do not immediately lower windows display scaling if magnifier caused the enlargement. practice: practice turning magnifier on and recovering. 26.2 colors look wrong what you will learn: check accessibility color features first. before you begin: colors suddenly look inverted or unusual. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+c if the color filter shortcut is enabled. press ctrl+alt+i if magnifier is on to check inversion. press windows+u and inspect color filters. inspect contrast themes. return each to the intended state. what should happen: the source of the color change is identified. if that does not happen: if colors remain wrong, inspect display-driver/hardware settings only after accessibility features are ruled out. practice: practice toggling and restoring a filter. 26.3 keyboard seems to ignore or delay keys what you will learn: check filter/sticky keys before assuming hardware failure. before you begin: typing feels delayed or modifiers stick. exactly how to do it press windows+u. open keyboard. check filter keys and sticky keys. turn off the recently enabled feature or reduce its timing. test in notepad. what should happen: normal keyboard response returns if an accessibility timing feature caused the issue. if that does not happen: if the problem persists with both features off, test another keyboard/application. practice: practice identifying filter keys. 26.4 no audio from one side what you will learn: check mono audio and output device. before you begin: important audio seems missing through one ear/channel. exactly how to do it press windows+u. open audio. turn mono audio on temporarily. replay the content. if still missing, check speaker/headphone connection and settings > system > sound output. what should happen: stereo information is combined into one channel when mono audio is on. if that does not happen: mono cannot fix a physically failed headset/speaker, but it can prevent left/right-only content from disappearing. practice: compare mono and stereo. 26.5 voice access does not understand commands what you will learn: check listening state, microphone, and language. before you begin: voice access is open. exactly how to do it confirm voice access is listening rather than sleeping/muted. open voice access settings and confirm the selected microphone/language. reduce background noise. speak one simple built-in command. open the voice access command guide. what should happen: recognition improves or the cause is isolated. if that does not happen: a language/model mismatch or poor microphone can make commands unreliable. practice: use three simple commands in a quiet room. 26.6 live captions do not appear what you will learn: check language setup and audio source. before you begin: live captions is open. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+l. confirm the caption window/bar is visible. check that the required language package finished installing. play clearly audible speech. check caption language/settings. restart live captions. what should happen: captions appear for supported audio. if that does not happen: not every language, device, or feature combination has identical support. practice: test with a clear recorded voice. 26.7 accessibility shortcut was triggered accidentally what you will learn: identify and disable only the shortcut if needed. before you begin: a feature keeps turning on unexpectedly. exactly how to do it open windows+u. open the feature's detailed settings. find its keyboard shortcut option. turn off only the shortcut if you still want the feature available manually. test the previously troublesome key sequence. what should happen: accidental activation stops while the feature remains available. if that does not happen: do not disable the entire accessibility feature if only its shortcut is the problem. practice: review sticky keys and color filter shortcut options. part 27 - independent practice course level 1 - accessibility hub ☐ open windows+u. ☐ navigate three categories. ☐ return to hub. ☐ search for an accessibility feature. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 2 - vision basics ☐ increase text size. ☐ change pointer size. ☐ enable text cursor indicator. ☐ restore preferred settings. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 3 - magnifier ☐ turn on/off. ☐ zoom. ☐ change view. ☐ use reading command. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 4 - color and contrast ☐ apply color filter. ☐ apply contrast theme. ☐ restore original appearance. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 5 - hearing ☐ enable mono audio. ☐ configure visual audio alert. ☐ extend notification duration. ☐ test live captions. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 6 - speech ☐ start voice access. ☐ open an app by voice. ☐ use voice typing. ☐ stop both features. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 7 - keyboard/input ☐ use osk. ☐ use sticky keys. ☐ inspect filter keys. ☐ use toggle keys. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 8 - pointer alternatives ☐ enable mouse keys. ☐ move pointer. ☐ locate eye control settings. ☐ review touch indicator. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 9 - focus ☐ reduce one visual effect. ☐ simplify one taskbar item. ☐ test do not disturb/focus. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 10 - screen reader ☐ start narrator. ☐ use input learning. ☐ open narrator settings. ☐ stop narrator. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 11 - recovery ☐ recover from accidental magnifier. ☐ recover from color filter. ☐ recover from filter keys. ☐ recover from hidden notifications. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. level 12 - independence ☐ create a personal accessibility profile. ☐ write down shortcuts. ☐ explain how to turn each feature off. ☐ restore the computer to intended settings. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which setting or shortcut to use. part 28 - quick reference core accessibility shortcuts task command / path accessibility settings windows+u narrator on/off windows+ctrl+enter narrator settings windows+ctrl+n magnifier on windows+plus magnifier off windows+escape magnifier settings windows+ctrl+m live captions windows+ctrl+l voice typing windows+h on-screen keyboard windows+ctrl+o color filters (if shortcut enabled) windows+ctrl+c contrast theme shortcut left alt+left shift+print screen magnifier reading task command / path start/pause/resume reading ctrl+alt+enter (default modifier) previous sentence ctrl+alt+h next sentence ctrl+alt+k stop reading any key invert magnifier colors ctrl+alt+i accessibility settings map area examples vision text size, visual effects, mouse pointer and touch, text cursor, magnifier, color filters, contrast themes, narrator hearing audio, hearing devices, captions interaction speech, keyboard, mouse, eye control part 29 - official microsoft resources discover windows accessibility features windows keyboard shortcuts for accessibility make mouse, keyboard, and other input devices easier to use make windows easier to hear get started with voice access use the on-screen keyboard make it easier to focus on tasks how to use magnifier reading final independence checklist ☐ i can open and navigate windows 11 accessibility settings. ☐ i can change text size, visual effects, pointer, and text cursor settings. ☐ i can use magnifier and magnifier reading. ☐ i can use color filters and contrast themes. ☐ i understand the role of narrator. ☐ i can turn on live captions. ☐ i can configure mono audio and visual audio alerts. ☐ i can find hearing-device settings. ☐ i can start and use voice access. ☐ i can use voice typing. ☐ i can use the on-screen keyboard. ☐ i can configure sticky keys, filter keys, and toggle keys. ☐ i can use mouse keys. ☐ i understand touch, pen, and eye-control accessibility options. ☐ i can reduce notifications and visual clutter for focus. ☐ i can use the accessibility flyout and sign-in accessibility controls. ☐ i understand windows hello accessibility/security considerations. ☐ i can combine accessibility features without creating shortcut conflicts. ☐ i understand privacy/security risks of speech, captions, and assistive technologies. ☐ i can recover from common accidental accessibility settings. most important habit: when windows suddenly behaves differently, check accessibility features before assuming something is broken. windows+u is the recovery starting point. identify the most recently changed feature, undo that change first, and test before changing anything else. return to all manuals

entries.title: Windows 11 Screen Reader Manual
entries.snippet: Windows 11 Screen Reader Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: windows 11 screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual windows 11 screen reader manual narrator, nvda, and jaws independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual is written directly to a person learning windows 11 with a screen reader. it assumes little or no prior experience and explains exactly what to press, what you should hear, and how to recover when the result is different. three screen readers: narrator is built into windows 11. nvda is a free third-party screen reader from nv access. jaws is a commercial screen reader from freedom scientific. their commands are not interchangeable. command labels: every procedure identifies whether a command belongs to windows, narrator, nvda, or jaws. how to use this manual begin with parts 1-12 even if you eventually plan to use nvda or jaws. these sections teach windows 11 keyboard navigation that all three screen readers rely on. do one action, stop, and listen to what changed before pressing another key. tab normally moves forward through controls. shift+tab moves backward. arrow keys normally move within lists, menus, radio-button groups, tree views, and text. enter activates many buttons, links, selected files, and menu commands. spacebar toggles checkboxes and many buttons. escape closes menus/dialogs or backs out of temporary interfaces. alt+tab switches among open applications. windows key opens start. windows+s opens search. learn windows keyboard navigation first, then add the commands for your chosen screen reader. table of contents part 1 - what a screen reader does part 2 - windows 11 keyboard foundations part 3 - start, search, taskbar, and switching apps part 4 - windows settings part 5 - file explorer part 6 - dialog boxes, menus, and common controls part 7 - reading and editing text part 8 - web browsing concepts part 9 - notifications, quick settings, and system tray part 10 - copy, cut, paste, rename, and delete part 11 - keyboard troubleshooting and recovery part 12 - choosing narrator, nvda, or jaws part 13 - narrator: start, stop, and narrator key part 14 - narrator: input learning and basic navigation part 15 - narrator: scan mode part 16 - narrator: reading text and views part 17 - narrator: web navigation part 18 - narrator: settings, speech, verbosity, and punctuation part 19 - narrator: braille part 20 - narrator: troubleshooting part 21 - nvda: start, stop, and nvda key part 22 - nvda: basic navigation and speech part 23 - nvda: browse mode and web navigation part 24 - nvda: settings, add-ons, and braille part 25 - nvda: troubleshooting part 26 - jaws: start, stop, and jaws key part 27 - jaws: basic reading and help part 28 - jaws: virtual cursor and web navigation part 29 - jaws: forms, lists, and windows explorer part 30 - jaws: settings, quick settings, and braille part 31 - jaws: troubleshooting part 32 - comparing narrator, nvda, and jaws part 33 - independent practice course part 34 - quick reference commands part 35 - official resources part 1 - what a screen reader does a screen reader converts information from the windows interface into speech and, when connected, refreshable braille. it follows keyboard focus, a screen-reader cursor, browse/scan mode, or another navigation system. focus is the windows control currently ready to receive input. a button performs an action. a checkbox can be checked or unchecked. a combo box lets you choose from a list. an edit field is where you type text. a dialog box asks for information or a decision. a screen reader usually announces both the control name and control type. part 2 - windows 11 keyboard foundations task command next control tab previous control shift+tab activate enter toggle checkbox/button spacebar move in list/menu arrow keys close/back escape context menu shift+f10 switch applications alt+tab close window alt+f4 2.1 navigate a window with tab what you will learn: move through controls without a mouse. before you begin: open settings or another simple windows app. exactly how to do it press tab once. listen to the focused control. press tab again. continue through five controls. press shift+tab twice to move backward. if focus enters a list, use up/down arrow. press escape if a menu opens accidentally. what should happen: focus moves from control to control. if that does not happen: if tab seems stuck, press escape once, then tab again. if focus is in a list, use arrow keys. practice: move forward ten controls and backward five. part 3 - start, search, taskbar, and switching apps 3.1 open an app from start/search what you will learn: launch programs without locating desktop icons. before you begin: be anywhere in windows. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type the app name, for example notepad. wait for search results. use up/down arrow if multiple results appear. press enter on the correct result. what should happen: the app opens. if that does not happen: if the wrong result opens, press alt+f4 and search using a more specific name. practice: open notepad, settings, and calculator. 3.2 switch between open apps what you will learn: move among running applications. before you begin: open at least two apps. exactly how to do it hold alt. press tab repeatedly while holding alt. listen to each app name. release alt on the desired app. what should happen: the selected app receives focus. if that does not happen: if it is not listed, it may not be open. practice: switch between notepad and settings three times. 3.3 use the taskbar what you will learn: reach pinned/running apps. before you begin: be anywhere in windows. exactly how to do it press windows+t. use left/right arrow through taskbar items. press enter to open or switch to the selected app. press escape when finished. what should happen: taskbar focus moves among apps. if that does not happen: if windows+t seems silent, press it again and listen for a taskbar item. practice: open one pinned app. part 4 - windows settings 4.1 open and search settings what you will learn: find a windows option efficiently. before you begin: be anywhere in windows. exactly how to do it press windows+i. wait for settings. tab to the search box if needed. type narrator, bluetooth, sound, or accessibility. use down arrow through results. press enter on the desired result. use tab/shift+tab through controls. what should happen: the requested settings page opens. if that does not happen: if the exact phrase is not found, search with a broader word. practice: find accessibility > narrator. part 5 - file explorer 5.1 open file explorer what you will learn: browse folders and files. before you begin: be anywhere in windows. exactly how to do it press windows+e. wait for file explorer. press tab through major panes. when focus is in the file list, use arrow keys through files. press enter to open a folder/file. press alt+left arrow to go back. press alt+up arrow to move up one folder. what should happen: you can enter and leave folders. if that does not happen: if arrow keys do not move files, press tab until the file list is focused. practice: open documents, enter a folder, then return. 5.2 rename a file or folder what you will learn: change an item's name. before you begin: select a practice item. exactly how to do it move to the item. press f2. type the new name. press enter. listen to confirm the new name. what should happen: the item is renamed. if that does not happen: if f2 does nothing, confirm the file itself is selected. practice: rename a practice file and rename it back. part 6 - dialog boxes, menus, and common controls button: enter or spacebar. checkbox: spacebar toggles. radio buttons: arrow keys. combo box: alt+down arrow opens, arrows choose, enter confirms. tabs: ctrl+tab / ctrl+shift+tab often changes tabs. context menu: shift+f10. menus: alt or f10 can expose menus in many desktop apps. 6.1 use a combo box what you will learn: choose an option in a drop-down. before you begin: focus is on a combo box. exactly how to do it press alt+down arrow. listen to the current item. press up/down arrow through choices. press enter on the desired choice. what should happen: the combo box closes with the selected value. if that does not happen: if it does not open, try spacebar or enter. practice: change a harmless option and restore it. part 7 - reading and editing text task command character left/right arrow word ctrl+left/right arrow line up/down arrow line start/end home / end document start/end ctrl+home / ctrl+end select word ctrl+shift+left/right arrow select all ctrl+a copy/cut/paste ctrl+c / ctrl+x / ctrl+v undo ctrl+z 7.1 type and correct a sentence what you will learn: use standard editing commands. before you begin: open notepad. exactly how to do it type: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. press ctrl+left arrow to move backward by word. press left/right arrow by character. use backspace/delete to remove text. type the correction. press ctrl+home. use your screen reader's reading command to review. what should happen: the correction occurs at the caret. if that does not happen: if the caret is lost, use ctrl+home or ctrl+end and navigate again. practice: create and correct three errors. part 8 - web browsing concepts narrator calls its webpage reading mode scan mode, nvda calls it browse mode, and jaws uses the virtual cursor. in these modes, single letters can jump to page structures instead of typing. tab moves among focusable links and form controls. enter activates. h often moves by heading. shift+h often moves backward by heading. typing fields require a typing/focus/forms mode rather than page-navigation mode. key idea: if letters navigate instead of typing, check the screen reader's reading mode. if letters type when you expected heading navigation, check whether you are in a typing/focus/forms mode. part 9 - notifications, quick settings, and system tray 9.1 open quick settings what you will learn: reach wi-fi, volume, bluetooth, and accessibility controls. before you begin: be anywhere in windows. exactly how to do it press windows+a. use tab and arrows through controls. press spacebar/enter to toggle or activate. press escape to close. what should happen: quick settings opens. if that does not happen: if it does not, verify the windows key is functioning. practice: open it, find volume, and close it. 9.2 open notification center what you will learn: review recent notifications. before you begin: be anywhere in windows. exactly how to do it press windows+n. use tab and arrows through notifications/calendar. press enter on a notification if desired. press escape to close. what should happen: notification center opens. if that does not happen: if there are no notifications, you may hear only date/calendar information. practice: open and close it. part 10 - copy, cut, paste, rename, and delete 10.1 copy and paste a file what you will learn: duplicate a file. before you begin: select a practice file. exactly how to do it press ctrl+c. navigate to the destination folder. press ctrl+v. wait for the copy. find the copied file. what should happen: the copied file appears. if that does not happen: if it does not, verify selection and destination permissions. practice: copy a practice file. 10.2 delete safely what you will learn: delete a selected item deliberately. before you begin: select a disposable practice file. exactly how to do it read the filename carefully. press delete. if asked to confirm, read the dialog before choosing yes. avoid shift+delete for practice because it bypasses normal recycle bin behavior. what should happen: the item is removed/moved to recycle bin. if that does not happen: if the wrong item is selected, press escape before confirming. practice: delete and restore a practice item. part 11 - keyboard troubleshooting and recovery press escape once or twice if focus seems trapped. use alt+tab away and back if an app's focus becomes confusing. use windows+s as a stable way to start another task. if typing fails on a webpage, inspect the screen reader's browse/scan/forms mode. if speech is silent, check system volume/output before changing many screen-reader settings. part 12 - choosing narrator, nvda, or jaws screen reader overview narrator built into windows 11; immediate access; no installation. nvda free/open-source; strong web and application support. jaws commercial; extensive training, office/web support, scripting, and enterprise use. backup strategy: even if nvda or jaws is your main screen reader, narrator can be valuable because it is built into windows. part 13 - narrator: start, stop, and narrator key task command start/stop narrator windows+ctrl+enter exit narrator narrator+esc narrator settings windows+ctrl+n narrator key caps lock or insert by default 13.1 start narrator what you will learn: turn on windows 11's built-in screen reader. before you begin: be at the keyboard. exactly how to do it hold windows and ctrl. press enter once. release all keys. listen for narrator speech. if narrator home opens, use tab through it or close/minimize it. what should happen: narrator announces the current item. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, press windows+ctrl+n and turn narrator on in settings. practice: start and stop narrator twice. part 14 - narrator: input learning and basic navigation task command input learning narrator+1 next item narrator+right arrow previous item narrator+left arrow primary action narrator+enter commands list narrator+f1 current-item commands narrator+f2 pass next key narrator+3 14.1 use input learning what you will learn: discover commands safely. before you begin: narrator is on. exactly how to do it press narrator+1. press a narrator command. listen to its description. try several commands. press narrator+1 again to turn input learning off. what should happen: narrator describes commands without normally executing them. if that does not happen: if commands act normally, input learning may be off. practice: identify next, previous, primary action, and scan mode. 14.2 move by narrator item what you will learn: use narrator's own item navigation. before you begin: narrator is on. exactly how to do it press narrator+right arrow. listen to the item. press it again. press narrator+left arrow to return. press narrator+enter on a harmless selected control. what should happen: narrator moves through items and activates the selected control. if that does not happen: if nothing changes, press tab to ensure the app has keyboard focus. practice: move through five items. part 15 - narrator: scan mode task command toggle scan mode narrator+spacebar primary action enter or spacebar next/previous paragraph p / shift+p next/previous line ctrl+down / ctrl+up next/previous word ctrl+right / ctrl+left next/previous character right / left first/last line ctrl+home / ctrl+end 15.1 use scan mode on a webpage what you will learn: read and navigate web content. before you begin: open edge, chrome, or firefox with narrator. exactly how to do it press narrator+spacebar if you need to confirm/toggle scan mode. press down arrow through content. press h to move to the next heading where supported. press shift+h for previous heading. press tab to a link or form control. press enter to activate. type normally when focus enters an edit field; scan mode may turn off automatically. use up/down arrow to leave the edit field and resume reading. what should happen: you can navigate page structure and enter text. if that does not happen: if letters type instead of navigate, scan mode may be off. practice: navigate by headings and links. part 16 - narrator: reading text and views task command change view narrator+page up / page down move in selected view narrator+left/right arrow time/date narrator+f12 battery/network narrator+shift+b screen curtain narrator+ctrl+c describe image narrator+ctrl+d webpage summary narrator+s 16.1 change narrator view what you will learn: navigate by word, line, paragraph, heading, link, or other unit. before you begin: narrator is on. exactly how to do it press narrator+page down until the desired view is announced. press narrator+right arrow to move forward in that view. press narrator+left arrow to move backward. change view again when needed. what should happen: movement follows the chosen unit. if that does not happen: some views exist only in certain contexts. practice: practice word, paragraph, and heading views. part 17 - narrator: web navigation scan mode turns on automatically in many supported browsers. narrator+s gives a webpage summary. narrator+ctrl+d can request an image description when an image is focused. g and shift+g can move among graphics/images in current scan mode support. 17.1 complete a web form what you will learn: move between reading and typing safely. before you begin: open a safe practice form. exactly how to do it navigate to an edit field. press enter/spacebar if needed. type text. press tab to the next control. press spacebar on checkboxes. use alt+down arrow for combo boxes. review before submitting. what should happen: you can type and navigate controls. if that does not happen: if letters jump around the page, verify focus and scan mode state. practice: complete a non-sensitive practice form. part 18 - narrator: settings, speech, verbosity, and punctuation 18.1 open narrator settings what you will learn: adjust narrator preferences. before you begin: narrator may be on or off. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+n. use tab through settings. review voice, speed, pitch, volume, verbosity, typing feedback, narrator key, and startup options. change one setting at a time. test and restore if needed. what should happen: narrator uses the changed setting. if that does not happen: if you become lost, close settings and reopen with windows+ctrl+n. practice: change speech rate slightly and restore it. narrator key: caps lock and insert both serve as the narrator key by default. part 19 - narrator: braille connect a compatible braille display by usb/bluetooth. open narrator settings > braille. configure the display and braille input/output tables. device-specific routing/panning commands vary. narrator+alt+b toggles the braille viewer. 19.1 verify braille what you will learn: confirm output, input, and routing. before you begin: connect a supported display. exactly how to do it move narrator with narrator+right arrow. confirm braille changes. open an edit field and type if display input is supported. use a routing key and confirm focus/caret movement. pan left/right with display controls. what should happen: output follows narrator and supported input/routing work. if that does not happen: if windows sees the display but narrator does not, check narrator braille settings and supported-display mappings. practice: perform output, input, routing. part 20 - narrator: troubleshooting 20.1 narrator is silent what you will learn: restore speech logically. before you begin: narrator should be running. exactly how to do it press windows+ctrl+enter to confirm state. check system volume/output. press tab or narrator+right arrow to trigger speech. open narrator settings with windows+ctrl+n. restart narrator. what should happen: speech returns. if that does not happen: if windows has no audio in any app, troubleshoot system sound. practice: memorize the sequence. part 21 - nvda: start, stop, and nvda key nvda is a free screen reader from nv access. the nvda modifier is commonly insert, caps lock, or both depending on settings. task command nvda menu nvda+n exit nvda+q input help nvda+1 stop speech ctrl say title nvda+t say focused object nvda+tab 21.1 start nvda what you will learn: launch nvda and verify it is active. before you begin: nvda must be installed. exactly how to do it press windows key. type nvda. press enter. wait for startup speech/sound. press nvda+n. press escape to close the menu. what should happen: nvda is running. if that does not happen: if search cannot find nvda, it may not be installed. practice: start nvda and open its menu. part 22 - nvda: basic navigation and speech 22.1 use nvda input help what you will learn: discover commands safely. before you begin: nvda is running. exactly how to do it press nvda+1. press keys/commands to identify. listen to nvda explain them. press nvda+1 again to turn input help off. what should happen: commands are described without normal action. if that does not happen: if actions occur, input help is not active. practice: identify nvda menu, quit, title, and focused-object commands. windows focus: nvda generally follows windows keyboard focus, so standard tab, arrows, enter, spacebar, windows search, and file explorer commands remain essential. part 23 - nvda: browse mode and web navigation task command next/previous heading h / shift+h heading level 1 through 6 next/previous link k / shift+k form field f / shift+f edit field e / shift+e button b / shift+b checkbox x / shift+x table t / shift+t landmark d / shift+d toggle browse/focus mode nvda+space 23.1 navigate a webpage with nvda what you will learn: use structural quick keys. before you begin: open a webpage with nvda. exactly how to do it press h for the next heading. press shift+h to move back. press k for next link. press f for next form field. press enter on an interactive item. if you need to type and remain in browse mode, press nvda+space to switch to focus mode. press nvda+space again to return when needed. what should happen: you can scan the page and type in fields. if that does not happen: if letters type when you expected navigation, you are likely in focus mode. practice: find a heading, link, and edit field. part 24 - nvda: settings, add-ons, and braille 24.1 open nvda settings what you will learn: adjust speech, keyboard, browse, and braille preferences. before you begin: nvda is running. exactly how to do it press nvda+n. open preferences > settings. use the category list to find speech, keyboard, browse mode, braille, or other settings. change one setting at a time. apply/ok. what should happen: nvda uses the new preference. if that does not happen: restore the old value if behavior worsens. practice: find speech and braille without changing them. add-ons: install add-ons only from trusted sources and verify compatibility with your current nvda release. part 25 - nvda: troubleshooting if nvda is silent, press ctrl, then navigate to trigger speech and check system audio. if letters navigate instead of typing, switch to focus mode with nvda+space. if letters type instead of navigating, return to browse mode with nvda+space. after an nvda update, test without optional add-ons if unusual behavior begins. use nvda+1 when you forget a command. part 26 - jaws: start, stop, and jaws key jaws traditionally uses insert as the jaws key in desktop layout. laptop layout commonly uses caps lock. task command keyboard help insert+1 context-sensitive help insert+f1 hot key help insert+h windows key help insert+w jaws command search insert+space, then j jaws window insert+j exit jaws insert+f4 26.1 start jaws what you will learn: launch jaws and verify it is active. before you begin: jaws must be installed and authorized as required. exactly how to do it press windows key. type jaws. press enter. wait for startup speech. press insert+t to hear the current window title. press insert+1 to enable keyboard help. press insert+1 again to turn it off. what should happen: jaws announces the active interface. if that does not happen: if jaws does not start, verify installation/authorization. practice: start jaws and identify the window title. part 27 - jaws: basic reading and help task command say word insert+numpad5 say line insert+up arrow window title insert+t current control/prompt insert+tab say font insert+f interrupt speech ctrl refresh screen insert+esc 27.1 use jaws help before guessing what you will learn: find commands from jaws itself. before you begin: jaws is running. exactly how to do it press insert+h for application hot keys. read the commands. press escape. press insert+w for common windows keys. press insert+space, then j for command search. what should happen: you can look up commands independently. if that does not happen: if one help method is not useful, use command search. practice: look up a web-navigation command. part 28 - jaws: virtual cursor and web navigation task command next heading h heading level 1 through 6 next link tab edit box e form control f button b checkbox x table t region r main region q headings list insert+f6 links list insert+f7 form fields list insert+f5 28.1 scan a webpage with jaws what you will learn: use quick keys and element lists. before you begin: open a webpage with jaws. exactly how to do it press h through headings. press shift+h backward. press insert+f6 for headings list. choose a heading and press enter. press insert+f7 for links list. choose a link and press enter. what should happen: you can jump directly to page structures. if that does not happen: if quick keys type into a field, forms mode may be active; return to the virtual cursor/browsing mode. practice: use both h and headings list on one page. part 29 - jaws: forms, lists, and windows explorer 29.1 fill a web form with jaws what you will learn: enter and exit forms mode correctly. before you begin: open a safe practice form. exactly how to do it press f or e to the desired field. press enter to enter forms mode if needed. type text. press tab to next control. use spacebar for checkboxes. use alt+down arrow/arrows/enter for combo boxes. press numpad plus in desktop layout to exit forms mode when needed. what should happen: you can type without quick-navigation letters taking over. if that does not happen: if h or other quick keys type after the form, exit forms mode. practice: complete a safe practice form. file explorer: useful windows explorer keys with jaws include f2 rename, delete, alt+enter properties, f5 refresh, tab/shift+tab between panes, and arrow keys through files. part 30 - jaws: settings, quick settings, and braille insert+v opens quick settings for the current application. insert+f2 opens jaws managers/tools. jaws supports many braille displays; device commands vary. use settings center/quick settings for verbosity, punctuation, typing echo, web behavior, braille, and application-specific behavior. 30.1 open quick settings what you will learn: change an application-specific option. before you begin: jaws is running in the target app. exactly how to do it press insert+v. search or move through settings. change only the intended option. confirm/close. test the application. what should happen: the option changes for that context. if that does not happen: restore the previous value if behavior worsens. practice: locate one setting without changing it. part 31 - jaws: troubleshooting press insert+esc to refresh screen information. use insert+1, insert+h, or command search when you forget a key. if web quick keys type into a field, exit forms mode/return to virtual cursor. test another browser before changing many jaws settings if one website behaves badly. review quick settings if an app-specific setting causes unexpected behavior. part 32 - comparing narrator, nvda, and jaws feature narrator nvda jaws built into windows yes no no cost included free commercial web mode scan mode browse mode virtual cursor command learning narrator+1 nvda+1 insert+1 common modifier caps lock/insert insert/caps lock insert desktop; caps lock often laptop do not mix commands: narrator+space toggles narrator scan mode; nvda+space toggles nvda browse/focus mode; jaws uses virtual cursor and forms mode controls. part 33 - independent practice course level 1 - windows keyboard ☐ open search. ☐ open notepad. ☐ use tab/shift+tab. ☐ switch apps with alt+tab. ☐ close with alt+f4. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 2 - settings and files ☐ open settings. ☐ search accessibility. ☐ open file explorer. ☐ enter/leave folders. ☐ rename a practice file. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 3 - text editing ☐ type a paragraph. ☐ move by word. ☐ select text. ☐ copy/paste. ☐ undo. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 4 - narrator ☐ start/stop narrator. ☐ use input learning. ☐ move next/previous item. ☐ toggle scan mode. ☐ navigate headings. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 5 - narrator advanced ☐ change view. ☐ open narrator settings. ☐ use webpage summary. ☐ test braille if applicable. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 6 - nvda ☐ start nvda. ☐ use input help. ☐ open nvda menu. ☐ navigate with h/k/f. ☐ toggle browse/focus mode. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 7 - jaws ☐ start jaws. ☐ use keyboard help. ☐ use insert+h. ☐ use heading/link lists. ☐ enter/exit forms mode. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. level 8 - recovery ☐ escape from a menu. ☐ recover when letters won't type. ☐ recover when letters type instead of navigate. ☐ identify which screen reader is active. ready to advance: you can complete every checked task without another person telling you which key to press. part 34 - quick reference commands windows 11 task command start windows key search windows+s settings windows+i file explorer windows+e quick settings windows+a notifications windows+n taskbar windows+t switch apps alt+tab close app alt+f4 context menu shift+f10 narrator task command start/stop windows+ctrl+enter settings windows+ctrl+n input learning narrator+1 next/previous narrator+right/left arrow primary action narrator+enter scan mode narrator+spacebar commands narrator+f1 exit narrator+esc nvda task command menu nvda+n exit nvda+q input help nvda+1 browse/focus mode nvda+space say title nvda+t focused object nvda+tab jaws task command keyboard help insert+1 context help insert+f1 hot key help insert+h windows key help insert+w command search insert+space, then j say title insert+t quick settings insert+v refresh screen insert+esc exit insert+f4 part 35 - official resources microsoft complete guide to narrator https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/accessibility/windows/narrator/complete-guide-to-narrator microsoft narrator scan mode https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/accessibility/windows/narrator/chapter-3-using-scan-mode microsoft narrator keyboard commands https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/appendix-b-narrator-keyboard-commands-and-touch-gestures-8bdab3f4-b3e9-4554-7f28-8b15bd37410a microsoft narrator braille https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/chapter-8-using-narrator-with-braille-3e5f065b-1c9d-6eb2-ec6d-1d07c9e94b20 nv access nvda user guide and key commands https://download.nvaccess.org/releases/stable/documentation/en/ freedom scientific jaws training https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/jaws/ freedom scientific jaws hotkeys https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/jaws/hotkeys/ final independence checklist ☐ i can navigate windows 11 using the keyboard. ☐ i can use start/search, settings, file explorer, taskbar, quick settings, and notifications. ☐ i can type and edit text without a mouse. ☐ i understand focus and browse/scan/forms modes. ☐ i can start/stop and use narrator. ☐ i understand narrator scan mode and views. ☐ i can use narrator braille if needed. ☐ i can start and use nvda if installed. ☐ i understand nvda browse and focus modes. ☐ i can start and use jaws if installed. ☐ i understand jaws virtual cursor and forms mode. ☐ i know how to use each screen reader's built-in help. ☐ i can troubleshoot common speech, focus, typing, and web-navigation problems. most important habit: always know which layer you are controlling: windows itself, narrator, nvda, or jaws. when a key behaves unexpectedly, first identify which screen reader and navigation mode are active. return to all manuals

entries.title: Zoom Manual
entries.snippet: Zoom Manual: step-by-step keyboard and screen-reader instructions, practice, troubleshooting, and command references.
entries.text: zoom manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual zoom manual meetings, chat, screen sharing, accessibility, and screen readers independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual official zoom workplace getting started guide purpose: this manual is written directly to the person learning zoom. it assumes you may be opening zoom for the first time. every procedure explains where to go, exactly what to click or press, what should happen, and what to do if the result is different. current interface: zoom states that the zoom workplace desktop interface was updated in version 6.7.0. this manual uses that current interface as its reference while explaining alternatives when a toolbar item is under more or has been customized. important: meeting features can be disabled or restricted by the host, account administrator, organization, license, or meeting policy. if a control described here is missing, that does not always mean you are doing something wrong. how to use this manual work through parts 1-8 first if zoom is completely new to you. do one action at a time, then stop and confirm what changed. tab moves forward through many buttons and fields. shift+tab moves backward. enter or spacebar activates many focused controls. escape closes many menus, dialogs, and temporary panels. windows and mac shortcuts are shown separately when they differ. screen-reader users should listen to both the control name and the control type before activating it. zoom lets users customize toolbar placement, and hosts/admins can restrict features. use the control name rather than assuming it is always in the same position. use zoom settings > keyboard shortcuts to review the exact shortcuts available in your installed version. table of contents part 1 - what zoom is part 2 - install, open, and sign in part 3 - learn the zoom workplace window part 4 - essential keyboard navigation part 5 - join a meeting from a link part 6 - join with meeting id and passcode part 7 - test audio, microphone, speaker, and camera part 8 - understand the meeting window part 9 - mute and unmute part 10 - start and stop video part 11 - participants part 12 - in-meeting chat part 13 - captions and accessibility part 14 - raise hand, reactions, and non-verbal feedback part 15 - share your screen or a window part 16 - leave a meeting part 17 - schedule a meeting part 18 - start a meeting you host part 19 - invite others part 20 - host and security controls part 21 - waiting room part 22 - breakout rooms part 23 - recording part 24 - zoom team chat part 25 - profile, status, and settings part 26 - keyboard shortcuts part 27 - windows screen reader use part 28 - voiceover on mac part 29 - zoom web app part 30 - zoom mobile app part 31 - troubleshooting part 32 - independent practice course part 33 - quick reference part 34 - official zoom resources part 1 - what zoom is zoom workplace is a collaboration application that can include meetings, team chat, phone, calendar, mail, whiteboard, and other tools depending on your account. this manual focuses primarily on the features most people need to participate independently in zoom meetings. a zoom meeting is an online session where participants can use audio, video, chat, captions, reactions, screen sharing, and other features. a host starts or controls the meeting. a co-host can be given many host controls. a participant joins the meeting and can use the controls allowed by the host. a waiting room can hold participants before the host admits them. a meeting id identifies a meeting. some meetings also require a passcode. a join link can contain enough information to open the correct meeting directly. zoom workplace desktop app is different from the zoom web portal. the desktop app is used for meetings and local app settings; the web portal contains many account-level settings. part 2 - install, open, and sign in 2.1 open zoom workplace on windows what you will learn: open zoom using only the keyboard. before you begin: zoom workplace must already be installed. exactly how to do it press the windows key. type zoom workplace. wait for the zoom workplace app to appear in windows search. press enter. wait for the zoom window to open. if the first screen gives you sign in, join a meeting, or sign up, choose sign in if you have an account and want access to your scheduled meetings/settings. use tab to move to sign in and press enter if necessary. enter the account information requested by zoom or your organization. complete any browser-based, single-sign-on, password, or verification prompts. return to the zoom workplace app and wait until its main window finishes loading. what should happen: the main zoom workplace window opens with your account signed in. if that does not happen: if zoom does not appear in windows search, it may not be installed. if your organization uses sso, make sure you choose the correct sign-in method rather than repeatedly entering a personal zoom password. practice: close zoom, reopen it from windows search, and identify whether you are signed in. 2.2 open zoom workplace on a mac what you will learn: open zoom from spotlight. before you begin: zoom workplace must already be installed. exactly how to do it press command+space. type zoom workplace. press return. wait for the app to open. use tab or voiceover navigation to move to sign in if needed. choose the correct sign-in method. complete password, browser, sso, or verification steps. return to zoom after authentication. what should happen: zoom workplace opens and displays the signed-in app. if that does not happen: if spotlight cannot find zoom workplace, check the applications folder or install the current zoom workplace app. practice: quit and reopen zoom once. part 3 - learn the zoom workplace window zoom's main app window can include home, meetings/calendar, team chat, contacts, whiteboards, and additional products. zoom notes that the desktop interface changed in version 6.7.0, so the exact navigation bar may differ from older instructions. navigation bar: switches among zoom products and work areas. home: shows upcoming meetings and common actions such as join, new meeting, or schedule. meetings or calendar: displays scheduled meetings/events depending on your account integration. team chat: displays zoom chat conversations and channels. profile picture/account menu: opens status, account controls, settings, and update options. settings: contains audio, video, accessibility, keyboard shortcuts, and other preferences. meeting window: opens separately when you start or join a meeting. 3.1 explore the zoom window with tab what you will learn: learn where keyboard focus moves before activating controls. before you begin: zoom workplace is open. exactly how to do it press tab once. listen to or visually identify the focused item. press tab again. continue through several controls. press shift+tab to move backward. when focus enters a list, try up arrow and down arrow to move within the list. press escape if you enter a temporary menu or pane that you do not want to use. continue until you can identify the navigation area, central content, and profile/settings controls. what should happen: you can move through the app without clicking random controls. if that does not happen: if tab appears to stop moving, try escape once, then tab again. if focus is inside a list, use arrow keys. practice: explore the home screen for two minutes without starting or joining a meeting. part 4 - essential keyboard navigation task windows mac mute/unmute audio alt+a command+shift+a temporarily unmute while holding space hold space while muted and meeting window has focus hold space while muted and meeting window has focus start/stop video alt+v command+shift+v start/stop screen share alt+s command+shift+s open/close in-meeting chat alt+h command+shift+h open/close participants alt+u command+u raise/lower hand alt+y option+y switch speaker/gallery view alt+f1 / alt+f2 where available use current zoom shortcut settings shortcut accuracy: zoom allows keyboard shortcuts to be viewed and edited in settings > keyboard shortcuts. if your installed version differs, trust the shortcut shown inside your zoom app. 4.1 find zoom's current keyboard shortcuts what you will learn: use zoom's own settings to verify a command. before you begin: be signed into the zoom workplace desktop app. exactly how to do it open your profile/account menu. choose settings. move to keyboard shortcuts. move through the list of shortcut actions. find the action you want, such as mute/unmute, start/stop video, participants, chat, or share screen. read the key combination assigned to it. if zoom allows editing and you intentionally want a different shortcut, change it carefully. close settings when finished. what should happen: you can verify the shortcut rather than relying on memory. if that does not happen: if keyboard shortcuts is not visible, update zoom workplace and make sure you are using the desktop app rather than a limited browser interface. practice: verify the shortcuts for audio, video, chat, participants, and screen sharing. part 5 - join a meeting from a link 5.1 join from an email or calendar link what you will learn: join the correct meeting and make deliberate audio/video choices before entering. before you begin: have the meeting invitation available. exactly how to do it open the invitation email or calendar event. move to the zoom join link. activate the link. if a browser asks whether to open zoom workplace, choose open zoom meetings/zoom workplace. if zoom is not installed, the browser may offer to download it or may provide an option to join from the browser. wait for the zoom pre-join screen. read the meeting name if shown so you know you are joining the correct session. check your display name. edit it if the meeting allows and if it is incorrect. check the microphone/audio choice. check the camera/video choice. when you are ready, activate join. if the meeting uses a waiting room, wait for the host to admit you. what should happen: you enter the correct meeting or waiting room. if that does not happen: if the link opens the wrong account or browser profile, close the meeting and reopen the invitation using the account expected by the organizer. if zoom says the meeting does not exist, verify that the link is complete and current. practice: use zoom's test meeting at zoom.us/test before an important first meeting. part 6 - join with meeting id and passcode 6.1 join without using a link what you will learn: enter a meeting id manually. before you begin: have the meeting id and passcode from the organizer. exactly how to do it open zoom workplace. on the initial or home screen, activate join. move to the meeting id field. type the meeting id exactly. spaces can be ignored if zoom formats the number automatically. move to the display-name field if shown and enter the name you want participants to see. choose whether to connect without audio or turn off your video before joining if those options are shown. activate join. if prompted, type the meeting passcode exactly. activate join meeting. wait for the meeting or waiting room. what should happen: you enter the meeting or waiting room using the id and passcode. if that does not happen: if zoom says the passcode is wrong, recheck uppercase/lowercase characters and make sure you did not confuse similar characters such as 0/o or 1/l. practice: practice opening the join dialog and identifying every field without actually joining. part 7 - test audio, microphone, speaker, and camera zoom provides a test meeting at zoom.us/test. zoom recommends using it to become familiar with meeting controls and test your microphone and speakers before a real meeting. 7.1 test your speaker what you will learn: confirm that meeting audio will come through the intended device. before you begin: connect your headphones, speakers, or headset. exactly how to do it open zoom settings from your profile/account menu. open audio settings. find the speaker device selection. read the currently selected device. open the device list if you need to change it. choose your desired headphones or speakers. activate test speaker. listen for the test sound. adjust the zoom or system output volume if needed. what should happen: you hear the zoom test sound through the intended device. if that does not happen: if you hear nothing, check system volume, mute state, cable/bluetooth connection, and whether zoom selected the wrong output device. practice: switch temporarily to a second available speaker device and then restore your preferred device. 7.2 test your microphone what you will learn: confirm that zoom can hear you. before you begin: connect the microphone or
